sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 2.6.4 and its proof, published p. 134; arXiv v3 p. 19 (Lemma 2.6.4); arXiv v1/v2 Lemma 2.5.4(2), p. 19
sourceIssues.printed: Lemma 2.6.4 assumes γ has order coprime to ℓ and asserts G_{S,γ} = θ_S^{−1} Hom_{O_λ}(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}). It considers (g^{−1}Ψ)h_γ ∈ Gal(F_S/F) = Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}) ⋊ Gal(F^{(m)}/F), and claims that the order assumption provides a lift γ̃ ∈ Gal(F̃_S/F⁺) of γ whose power γ̃^{[F:F⁺]} ∈ Gal(F̃_S/F) maps to (g^{−1}Ψ)h_γ in Gal(F_S/F).
sourceIssues.correction: Replace the equality by the inclusion G_{S,γ} ⊆ θ_S^{−1}Hom_{O_λ}(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}). Exactly, G_{S,γ} = q(N^α), where N = Gal(F̃_S/F₊^{(m)}), α is conjugation by a lift σ₀ of γ of prime-to-ℓ order, and q is restriction to F_S. Equality holds if [F:F⁺] = 1. For [F:F⁺] = 2, the statement Proposition 2.6.6 actually needs is that the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains λ^c Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) with c independent of m. It holds with c = 𝔣(r_S)r_{Ind R} when R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠. When R extends to R₊ over F⁺, it holds for S inside a 𝔠-eigenspace ε exactly when γ acts on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} ⊂ R̄₊^{(m)} by ε, and it fails otherwise (then G_{S,γ} = {1} if S lies in the other eigenspace).
sourceIssues.reason: Take F+=Q(√5), F=F+(i), ell=3, m=1, R=Z3(1), j=2 and the identity polarization (muΦ=1). Let u=(1+√5)/2 and S be its one-dimensional mod-3 Kummer class, coming from the integral finite unit class. F(m)=F(m)+=F(ζ3); its degree over F+ is four, so u remains a noncube (use the fundamental-unit description of Q(√5)). FS=F(m)(cuberoot(u)) has cyclic cubic kernel. Choose γ induced by complex conjugation, of order two; hγ=1. Complex conjugation fixes the real cuberoot and inverts ζ3, so every lift of γ has square one. All associated-prime evaluations are consequently zero, while the right side is the full cubic kernel. The Kummer/Bloch–Kato unit identification is an explicit external input to this arithmetic witness, not claimed newly formalized. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — checked on the page image of p. 134 (Lemma 2.6.4 and its proof) with the definitions on p. 133; the counterexample was re-derived independently, and the exact replacement formula G_{S,γ} = q(N^α) was re-proved. The lemma is correct when [F:F⁺] = 1 and false in general when [F:F⁺] = 2. Counterexample to the printed lemma (all hypotheses of Proposition 2.6.6 also hold). F⁺ = ℚ(√5), F = ℚ(√5, i) (ℓ = 3 unramified), E_λ = ℚ₃, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, Ξ the identity ℤ₃(1)^𝔠 = ℤ₃(1)^∨(2), μ_Ξ = 1, B = 1, so ρ₊(𝔠) = (1, 1, 𝔠). Fix m ⩾ 1; u = (1+√5)/2. S := ℤ/3^m·κ(u) ⊆ H¹(F, μ_{3^m}) (Kummer class) lies in H¹_{f,R}(F, R̄^{(m)}) (u is a unit) and is free of rank one (u is not a cube in F: units of F are μ₄ × ⟨η⟩ with η = u or η² = ζu). ρ̄₊^{(m)}|_{Γ_F} = (ε̄, ε̄², 1), so F^{(m)} = F₊^{(m)} = F(ζ_{3^m}); Res is injective by Lemma 2.3.5(a) (ε̄(Γ_F) = 𝔽₃^× ∋ −1 as ζ₃ ∉ F), so K = Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}) ≅ ℤ/3^m with F_S = F(ζ_{3^m}, u^{1/3^m}), which is Galois over F⁺. γ := ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠) = (1, 1, 𝔠) has order 2 and h_γ = 1, so the printed right-hand side is all of K. Every lift σ of γ to Gal(F_S/F⁺) is τ·𝔠 with τ ∈ K, and 𝔠τ𝔠^{−1} = τ^{−1} (𝔠 fixes the real root u^{1/3^m} and inverts ζ_{3^m}); hence σ² = 1 and Ψ_{w^{(m)}} = σ^{2g} = 1 for every γ-associated place: G_{S,γ} = {1} ≠ K. Direct check: such places lie over primes v of F⁺ with ‖v‖ ≡ 2 mod 3, where every element of 𝔽_{‖v‖}^× is a 3^m-th power, so Frobenius fixes u^{1/3^m}. Mechanism in general: for [F:F⁺] = 2 the Frobenius at the inert place is σ^{2g}, and squares of lifts in the 𝔠-coset are constrained (σ² = (1+α)(n)·σ₀²). The step 'it is easy to see' asserts the opposite. (The displayed splitting Gal(F_S/F) = Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}) ⋊ Gal(F^{(m)}/F) is also unjustified, though only a prime-to-ℓ lift of ⟨h_γ⟩ is needed.) Relevance to the main theorems: in Theorem 1.1.1 R = R₀ ⊗ R₁ is restricted from F⁺, so H¹(F, R̄) splits into 𝔠-eigenspaces; for S in one eigenspace F_S is Galois over F⁺, σ₀ acts on K ⊆ Hom(S, R̄) through the action of the lift of γ on R̄, and G_{S,γ} = θ_S^{−1}Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ, γ=+1}); if γ acts by −1 on the h_γ-fixed line, G_{S,γ} = {1} and loc_w(S) = 0 at every γ-associated place, so no abundant element exists. Case for the defence: the inclusion ⊆ is correct; the lemma is correct for [F:F⁺] = 1, the setting of [46, Lemmas 5.7–5.8] that v1/v2 cited; in the Rankin–Selberg application with R ≇ R^𝔠 the needed disjointness may well hold, and in the base-change case one can probably choose γ with the right sign using the large image — but none of this is in the paper, which applies the lemma as stated. Reach: a stated result (Lemma 2.6.4, and Proposition 2.6.6 which relies on it, are false when [F:F⁺] = 2); the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2 and 8.3.2 (hence Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7, 1.1.9) invoke Proposition 2.6.6 with [F:F⁺] = 2 and need repair). Independent check 1: Quotation checked on the page image (p. 134 = PDF p. 28; definitions p. 133). HYPOTHESES IN FORCE. F ⊂ ℂ a number field on which 𝔠 restricts to an automorphism of order ≤ 2, F⁺ = F^{𝔠=1} (pp. 129–130); ℓ odd and unramified in F (p. 121); R ∈ Mod(F,O_λ)_fr nonzero with a j-polarization Ξ: R^𝔠 ≅ R^∨(j), Ξ^{𝔠,∨}(j) = (−1)^{μ_Ξ+j+1}Ξ (Def. 2.5.3); ρ₊ as in Constr. 2.5.4 (for [F:F⁺]=2: ρ₊|_{Γ_F} = (ρ, ε_ℓ^j, 1), ρ₊(𝔠) = (B, (−1)^{μ_Ξ+j+1}, 𝔠)); F^{(m)}, F₊^{(m)} the fixed fields of ker ρ̄^{(m)}, ker ρ̄₊^{(m)}; γ ∈ (GL_N × (O_λ/λ^m)^×, 𝔠) ∩ im ρ̄₊^{(m)} (for [F:F⁺]=2 the non-identity coset), h_γ = first component of γ^{[F:F⁺]} (Not. 2.6.2); S a f.g. O_λ-submodule of H¹_{f,R}(F, R̄^{(m)}); F_S/F^{(m)} and the injective equivariant θ_S from §2.3 with ρ = ρ̄^{(m)}; γ-associated places (Def. 2.6.3): places of F₊^{(m)} not over ∞ℓ, unramified over F⁺, with underlying place of F^{(m)} unramified in F_S, and Frobenius γ in Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F⁺); G_{S,γ} = their Frobenii Ψ_{w^{(m)}} in Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}). Lemma 2.6.4 adds only: order of γ prime to ℓ. THE EXAMPLE SATISFIES ALL OF THEM. F = ℚ(√5,i) ⊂ ℂ, 𝔠|_F ≠ 1, F⁺ = ℚ(√5), 3 unramified (disc 400). R = ℤ₃(1), Ξ = id (R^𝔠 = ℤ₃(1) = R^∨(2)); in rank one BᵗB^{−1} = 1 forces (−1)^{μ_Ξ+j+1} = 1 (μ_Ξ = 1), ρ₊(𝔠) = (1,1,𝔠), and ρ₊(𝔠g𝔠) = ρ₊(𝔠)ρ₊(g)ρ₊(𝔠) checks. S = ℤ/3^m·κ(u) ⊂ H¹_{f,R}(F, μ_{3^m}) (u = (1+√5)/2 a unit), free of rank one because u is not a cube in F (μ_F = μ₄, unit index ≤ 2) and F has no 3-power roots of unity. F^{(m)} = F₊^{(m)} = F(ζ_{3^m}); F_S = F(ζ_{3^m}, u^{1/3^m}) is Galois over F⁺ and K := Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}) ≅ ℤ/3^m (Res injective by Lemma 2.3.5(a): −1 ∈ ε̄(Γ_F) as √−3 ∉ F). γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠) has order 2, h_γ = 1, so the right-hand side of the lemma is all of K. RECOMPUTATION OF G_{S,γ}. A γ-associated place lies over v with Frob_v = complex conjugation on F(ζ_{3^m}), i.e. ‖v‖ ≡ 3 mod 4 and ‖v‖ ≡ −1 mod 3^m (so v has degree 1 over ℚ and is inert in F); w^{(m)} has residue field 𝔽_{‖v‖²} and Ψ_{w^{(m)}} acts on u^{1/3^m} by u^{(‖v‖²−1)/3^m} = (u^{‖v‖−1})^{(‖v‖+1)/3^m} ≡ 1, since u mod v lies in 𝔽_{‖v‖}. So G_{S,γ} = {1} ≠ K (smallest case m = 1, p = 11: u ∈ 𝔽₁₁, u^{40} = 1 in 𝔽₁₂₁). Group-theoretically: every lift of γ is τ𝔠 with 𝔠τ𝔠 = τ^{−1}, so (τ𝔠)² = 1. FAILING STEP. 'It is easy to see that there is γ̃ lifting γ with γ̃^{[F:F⁺]}|_{F_S} = (g^{−1}Ψ)h_γ' is false for [F:F⁺] = 2: squares of the coset σ₀N are (1+α)(N)·σ₀², a constrained set. Re-proved general formula: G_{S,γ} = {σ^{2g}|_{F_S} : σ ∈ σ₀N} = q(N_{2g}(N)) = q(N^α) (σ₀^{2g}|_{F_S} is a prime-to-ℓ element of the ℓ-group K, hence 1; q∘α^{2g} = q; on N^{α^{2g}}, N_{2g} is 2g/k times the norm of a cyclic group of order k prime to ℓ). For [F:F⁺] = 1, F₊^{(m)} = F^{(m)} (the perfect pairing R̄×R̄ → O/λ^m(j) forces ker ρ̄ ⊂ ker ε̄^j), N = K, α acts through h_γ, and the lemma holds; the inclusion ⊆ (first paragraph of the proof) always holds. The displayed ⋊ splitting is also unjustified but harmless (Schur–Zassenhaus gives a prime-to-ℓ lift of ⟨h_γ⟩). STRUCTURE FOR [F:F⁺] = 2. With M := Ind_F^{F⁺} R̄^{(m)}, Shapiro gives a Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F⁺)-equivariant injection θ̃: N ↪ Hom(S, M) (ker ρ̄_M = ker ρ̄₊), M^γ ≅ R̄^{h_γ} via the first projection, and θ_S(G_{S,γ}) = pr₁(θ̃(N)^γ). (i) If R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠, M_ℚ is absolutely irreducible and Res for M is injective (H¹(Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F), R̄) = 0 because Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F^{(m)}) is central and R̄^{Γ_F} = 0 under Lemma 2.3.5). Lemmas 2.3.3–2.3.4 for (F⁺, M) then show that the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains λ^{𝔣(r_S)r_M}Hom(S, R̄^{h_γ}). The printed equality can still fail, but this span statement is what Prop. 2.6.6 uses. (ii) If R = R₊|_{Γ_F} and S lies in the ε-eigenspace H¹(F⁺, R̄₊⊗η^{(1−ε)/2}) while γ acts on the line R̄^{h_γ} ⊂ R̄₊ by −ε, then H¹_ur(F⁺_v, R̄₊⊗η^{(1−ε)/2}) ≅ (R̄₊⊗η^{(1−ε)/2})^{φ_v} = 0 at every γ-associated v. So loc_w(S) = 0 and G_{S,γ} = {1}. The polarization sign plays no role: γ only fixes a Galois coset, and the sign is that of ρ̄_{R₊}(σ) on ker(ρ̄(σ²) − 1). VERSIONS: v1/v2 Lemma 2.5.4(2) (hypothesis: order of h_γ prime to ℓ) is proved only by reference to [Liu16, Lemmas 5.7–5.8] (a setting with [F:F⁺] = 1); v3 is identical to the published text. Independent check 2: Quote checked on the page images: p. 134 (PDF 28) for the lemma and proof; pp. 132–133 for Def. 2.5.3, Constr. 2.5.4, Not. 2.6.1–2.6.2 and Def. 2.6.3; pp. 121 and 129 for the standing assumptions of §2. v3 is identical. v1/v2 have Lemma 2.5.4(2), proved by citing [46, Lemmas 5.7–5.8], which treat the case [F:F⁺] = 1. Defence attempted; it fails at every point. (i) Scope. §2 asks only that ℓ be odd and unramified in F (p. 121) and that F ⊂ ℂ be 𝔠-stable (p. 129). ℓ = 3 and F = ℚ(√5,i) qualify. Any odd ℓ unramified in F with ζ_ℓ ∉ F works the same way (e.g. ℓ = 7). (ii) j and the polarization. Def. 2.5.3 allows any integer j. The map Ξ = id: ℤ₃(1)^𝔠 = ℤ₃(1) → ℤ₃(1)^∨(2) is Γ_F-equivariant. Also B·ᵗB⁻¹ = 1 = (−1)^{μ_Ξ+j+1} with μ_Ξ = 1. So ρ₊(𝔠) = (1,1,𝔠), and ρ₊ is a homomorphism: 𝔠(g,μ)𝔠 = (μ·ᵗg⁻¹,μ) gives ε²·ε⁻¹ = ε = ρ(𝔠g𝔠). (iii) γ and h_γ. γ := ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠) lies in the image and in the 𝔠-coset, and has order 2. h_γ is the first component of γ², which is 1, so (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = R̄^{(m)} is free of rank 1. The paper itself takes γ to be the image of g^{[F′:F⁺]}𝔠 in Prop. 2.7.2. (iv) The class S. Any finitely generated submodule of H¹_{f,R}(F,R̄^{(m)}) is allowed; no 𝔠-condition is imposed, and 𝔠 does not even act on H¹(F,R̄) in general. κ(u) lies in H¹_{f,R} because u is a unit. u is not a cube in F: if u = x³ then (x/𝔠x)³ = 1 and ζ₃ ∉ F, so x ∈ F⁺, but u is the fundamental unit of ℚ(√5). So S ≅ ℤ/3^m. (v) The field F_S. F^{(m)} = F₊^{(m)} = F(ζ_{3^m}). Res is injective by Lemma 2.3.5(a), since −1 ∈ ε̄(Γ_F). So F_S = F(ζ_{3^m}, u^{1/3^m}) and K := Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}) ≅ ℤ/3^m, with θ_S bijective. Recomputation of G_{S,γ}. A γ-associated place lies over a place v of F⁺ whose Frobenius σ ∈ Gal(F_S/F⁺) restricts to 𝔠 on F(ζ_{3^m}). w^{(m)} has residue degree 2 over v, so Ψ_{w^{(m)}} = σ². Write σ = τ𝔠 with τ ∈ K. Since 𝔠 fixes the real root u^{1/3^m} and inverts ζ_{3^m}, 𝔠τ𝔠 = τ⁻¹ and σ² = 1. Hence G_{S,γ} = {1}, whereas θ_S⁻¹Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) = K ≅ ℤ/3^m. Direct check. Such v have ‖v‖ = q ≡ −1 mod 3^m; for m = 1, v | 11 gives u ≡ 8, a cube in 𝔽₁₁. Since 3 ∤ q−1, u is a 3^m-th power in 𝔽_q, and all roots of X^{3^m} − u lie in 𝔽_{q²}. So w^{(m)} splits completely in F_S. General mechanism, re-derived. Let N := Gal(L/F₊^{(m)}), where L is the Galois closure of F_S·F₊^{(m)} over F⁺. Take σ₀ a lift of γ of order d prime to ℓ (Schur–Zassenhaus), α conjugation by σ₀, and q: N → K the restriction. Every lift is nσ₀, and σ₀^{2g}|_{F_S} = 1, so Ψ = q(Σ_{i<2g} α^i n). This gives G_{S,γ} = q(N)^α = q(N^α): the invariants of α, not of α² = h_γ. The step 'it is easy to see that there is an element γ̃ … lifting γ' asserts the opposite. What stands. The inclusion ⊆ (first paragraph of the proof) is correct, and the lemma is correct when [F:F⁺] = 1. The first reading's formula and correction are right. On reach, I refine the first reading's 'case for the defence'. When R ≅ R^𝔠, the failure is not confined to a badly chosen γ. For a rank-2 S with one class in each 𝔠-eigenspace, Proposition 2.6.6 fails for every γ. So Theorem 8.3.2 needs two γ's of opposite signs, not merely a well-chosen one. Reach to the main theorems: Lemma 2.6.4 reaches §8 only through Proposition 2.6.6. That proposition is invoked in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 (r_S = 1, p. 310) and of Theorem 8.3.2 (r_S = 2, p. 317), with R = R₀⊗R₁, Ξ = Ξ₀⊗Ξ₁ (j = 1), [F:F⁺] = 2. In both proofs γ comes from an arbitrary (γ₀,γ₁,ξ) supplied by (L5-2)/Lemma 2.7.1, satisfying (a)–(e), and is chosen without reference to S. If R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠, the span version above (constant r_{Ind R} instead of r_R) rescues Proposition 2.6.6, and the proofs go through with changed constants. If R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠 the application inherits the failure. This covers every instance of Theorem 1.1.1 (R = (Sym^{n₀−1}H¹(A₀)⊗Sym^{n₁−1}H¹(A₁))(n)|_{Γ_F}) and base-change pairs in Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. There H¹_f(F,R) = H¹_f(F⁺,R₊) ⊕ H¹_f(F⁺,R₊⊗η). Concretely, in the setting of Theorem 1.1.1 with ℓ large, suppose σ gives a γ satisfying (a)–(e). Then so does στ, for τ ∈ Gal(F̄/F_rflx) with ρ_{A₀}(τ) ≡ −1, ρ_{A₁}(τ) ≡ 1 and ε(τ) ≡ 1 mod ℓ^m (such τ exists by Serre's open image theorem): h_γ and ξ are unchanged, and the sign flips because n₀−1 is odd. For the hypothetical S that the proof by contradiction must exclude, lying in one eigenspace, one of these two admissible choices of γ gives loc_𝔭(S) = 0 at every γ-associated 𝔭. Then no abundant Ψ exists, ⟨s₁,c₁⟩_𝔭 = 0, and no contradiction follows. So the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2 and 8.3.2, and hence of Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9, have a gap in the self-conjugate case. For Theorem 1.1.1 the gap is repairable for all but finitely many ℓ: take S in one eigenspace and γ of matching sign. In rank one, if the Selmer group meets both eigenspaces, no single γ gives an abundant pair, so use γ at 𝔭₁ and γτ at 𝔭₂ (conditions (PI)/(PII) depend only on h_γ and ξ). For general admissible λ (Definition 8.1.1) and base-change pairs, (L5-2) supplies only one γ, and nothing in (L1)–(L7) guarantees one of the opposite sign. There the proofs of Theorems 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9 are incomplete as written. No main theorem is shown false. The defect only makes a particular γ useless, and the statements remain consistent with BBK: e.g. a rank-one configuration with Selmer rank one in each eigenspace would violate parity. Theorems 8.2.2 and 8.3.2 apply Proposition 2.6.6, and so this lemma, with [F:F⁺] = 2, R = R₀⊗R₁ and j = 1. The γ comes from (L5-2) via Lemma 2.7.1 and is chosen after S, with no condition tying it to S (page images pp. 310, 317–319). Nothing in the Rankin–Selberg setup, the 1-polarization or Definition 8.1.1 rules out the failure. Case R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠. This covers all of Theorem 1.1.1 (A and A′ are over F⁺: Lemma 8.1.3, Prop. 2.7.2) and base-change instances of 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. The lattice R is then Γ_{F⁺}-stable (call it R⁺), ℓ is odd, and H¹(F,R̄^{(m)}) = H¹(F⁺,R̄⁺) ⊕ H¹(F⁺,R̄⁺⊗η), with the local conditions preserved. For S in the χ-eigenspace, F_S is Galois over F⁺, and a cocycle computation gives θ_S(σ₀xσ₀⁻¹) = χ(σ₀)ρ⁺(σ₀)∘θ_S(x). Hence G_{S,γ} = θ_S⁻¹Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{χ(σ₀)ρ⁺(σ₀)=1}). The module (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} is a line (Lemma 2.7.1(c)), and ρ⁺(σ₀) acts on it by a sign ε₀. So G_{S,γ} is either all of θ_S⁻¹Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) or {1}. In the second case θ_S(Ψ_w)(s) = 0 at every γ-associated w. Restriction from F_w to F^{(m)}_{w^{(m)}} has degree g, which is prime to ℓ, so loc_w(s) = 0 in H¹_ns(F_w,R̄^{(m)}) ≅ R̄^{(m)}/(h_γ−1). Consequence for 8.2.2. The prime 𝔭 is γ-associated, so ⟨s₁,c₁⟩_𝔭 = 0 and no contradiction arises: the argument does not bound that eigenspace. Nothing controls the sign. For example, with n = 2 and the element g^{[F′:F⁺]}𝔠 of Prop. 2.7.2 (taking ρ̄(g) to commute with ρ⁺(𝔠)), one finds ε₀ = −c₁, where c₁ = ±1 is the eigenvalue of 𝔠 on the a-eigenvector of ρ̄_{A₀}(g). The paper leaves this free, and both choices satisfy (a)–(e). Consequence for 8.3.2. Suppose the hypothetical rank-2 S is ⟨s₊,s₋⟩, with one class in each eigenspace. Then every element of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) kills s₋ or kills s₊, for every γ, so no abundant pair exists. The paper uses a single γ for both 𝔭₁ and 𝔭₂. Repair. In rank 0, choose γ according to the eigenspace of S. In rank 1, use γ's of opposite signs at 𝔭₁ and 𝔭₂, as Bertolini–Darmon do when they choose ε_p. Changing the sign keeps h_γ and ξ, so conditions (a)–(e) and (PI)/(PII) are unaffected, since those are stated through Satake parameters at inert primes. For Theorem 1.1.1 both signs exist when ℓ ≫ 0: choose g in Prop. 2.7.2, or multiply by ρ̄₊(τ) with ρ̄(τ) = (−1)⊗1, which lies in the image since the image contains SL₂×SL₂ (Serre). So Theorem 1.1.1 survives with a modified proof. Not covered. For 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 at an arbitrary admissible λ, Definition 8.1.1 guarantees only one element satisfying (a)–(e). For 1.1.7, Lemma 8.1.4 supplies only ρ̄₊(φ_𝔭) at one prime 𝔭. So in the base-change case those proofs are incomplete unless a γ of the other sign is shown to exist, by an added hypothesis or a large-image argument. Case R_ℚ ≇ R_ℚ^𝔠. F_S and its 𝔠-conjugate should be linearly disjoint over F^{(m)} up to bounded index, because Hom_{Γ_F}(R,R^𝔠) = 0. A version of the lemma that loses only a bounded power of λ is then plausible, but the paper does not prove it. No main theorem is shown false. What fails is a proof by contradiction about a hypothetical Selmer class, and the statements are what Bloch–Kato predicts.

review.reason: Checked on p. 134 (and the definitions on p. 133). The first half of the proof gives θ_S(G_{S,γ}) ⊆ Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}); the converse step fails. In the counterexample (F⁺ = ℚ(√5), F = F⁺(i), ℓ = 3, m = 1, R = ℤ₃(1), γ = ρ̄₊(c), h_γ = 1, S spanned by the Kummer class of u = (1+√5)/2) every lift of γ to Gal(F̃_S/F⁺) = Gal(F⁺(i, ζ₃, u^{1/3})/F⁺) has the form cτ^k with cτc = τ⁻¹ (c inverts ζ₃ and fixes the real cube root), so its square is 1 and every Frobenius w(m) is trivial: G_{S,γ} = {1}, while θ_S⁻¹Hom(S, R̄) is all of Gal(F_S/F^{(m)}) ≅ ℤ/3 (u is not a cube, since x³ − u is irreducible over ℚ(√5) and F(ζ₃) has 2-power degree). sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts that any (S, γ)-abundant r-tuple (Ψ₁, …, Ψ_r) admits an S-basis {s₁, …, s_r} satisfying θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j) = 0 for i ≠ j and exp_λ(θ_S(Ψ_j)(s_j), (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) ⩾ m − m₀ − 𝔣(r)r_R. It regards the first assertion as immediate from Definition 2.6.5.
sourceIssues.correction: Assume 𝔣(r)r_R = 0 (e.g. R̄ absolutely irreducible and r_R minimal), or weaken to: there are elements s_j := Ce_j with AC = λ^c·I (a submodule containing λ^cS), or state it for a suitably chosen tuple rather than every abundant one. The application needs only one good pair, which exists when the O_λ-span of θ_S(G_{S,γ}) is large (cf. E1). At Proof of Theorem 8.3.2, (8.11), published pp. 317–318: Use only what abundance gives: after possibly interchanging Ψ1 and Ψ2, exp_λ θ_S(Ψ1)(λ0^{m_Σ−m_per}s) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R, and there is a primitive t ∈ S with θ_S(Ψ1)(t) = 0 and exp_λ θ_S(Ψ2)(t) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R; replace s2 by t in the rest of the proof.
sourceIssues.reason: Over O/λ^m with m>4, A=[[λ,1],[0,λ]] has image containing λ²O² and hence λ⁴O². Its total image has index |k|² but its two coordinate projections have indices 1 and |k|; a diagonal matrix with those projections would have index |k|. Right multiplication by a basis change preserves the image, so cannot diagonalize it. Thus the claimed implication from Definition 2.6.5 is false for general linear maps. This example is not presented as a realized Selmer evaluation system, so the finding is a proof gap rather than a counterexample under every global hypothesis. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): revised — confirmed that the inference is invalid, but it is an error in the stated first part of Proposition 2.6.7 (asserted for EVERY abundant tuple), not only a proof gap; the counterexample matrix is realizable whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) is all of Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}). Locator is Proposition 2.6.7 (not 2.6.6). Over O_λ/λ^n with n ⩾ 2, A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has det λ², image {(λx+y, λy)} ⊇ λ²(O_λ/λ^n)², of index |k|²; its coordinate projections have indices 1 and |k|, so a diagonal matrix with the same image would have index |k|. Column operations (change of basis of S) preserve the image, so no basis diagonalizes A. This A is abundant as soon as 𝔣(2)r_R = 4r_R ⩾ 2, i.e. r_R ⩾ 1 (r_R is any bound from Lemma 2.3.3, and is ⩾ 1 whenever R̄ is reducible). It is realized by actual Frobenius elements whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) = Hom(S, (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) (e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds, and θ_S surjective). Case for the defence: in the application the authors are free to choose the pair (Ψ₁, Ψ₂), and a suitable choice (or the one-sided variant) suffices for Theorem 8.3.2 — but the proposition as stated, and its proof, are wrong, and the choice requires control of G_{S,γ} that E1 removes. Reach: a stated result (first part of Proposition 2.6.7; the second part depends on it); the proof of Theorem 8.3.2 (Theorem 1.1.9), which uses it with r = 2). Independent check 1: Quotation checked on p. 135 (PDF p. 29): 'For every (S,γ)-abundant r-tuple … one can choose a basis {s₁,…,s_r} of S such that θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j) = 0 if i ≠ j and exp_λ(θ_S(Ψ_j)(s_j), (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) ⩾ m − m₀ − 𝔣(r)r_R' with proof 'The first part is obvious from Definition 2.6.5'. The statement is universally quantified over abundant tuples. Definition 2.6.5 (p. 134) asks only that the image of s ↦ (θ_S(Ψ_i)(s))_i contain λ^{m₀+𝔣(r)r_R}((R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ})^{⊕r}. Normalizing by λ^{m₀} (the values lie in λ^{m₀}O/λ^m because S is killed by λ^{m−m₀}), this says: the matrix A ∈ M_r(O/λ^n), n = m − m₀, has image ⊇ λ^c(O/λ^n)^r with c = 𝔣(r)r_R. A change of basis of S acts by A ↦ AC and preserves the image, so a diagonalizing basis exists iff im A is a product of coordinate submodules. Checked: A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] has Smith form diag(1,λ²), image of index |k|² containing λ²(O/λ^n)², while its coordinate projections are O/λ^n and λO/λ^n (a product would have index |k|). So it is abundant when c ⩾ 2 and not diagonalizable. Also A = [[1,0],[1,λ]] with image {(a,b): a ≡ b mod λ} ⊇ λ(O/λ^n)² is abundant as soon as c ⩾ 1. Does Definition 2.6.5 allow such matrices? It needs c = 𝔣(r)r_R ⩾ 1, i.e. r_R ⩾ 1, and rows that lie in θ_S(G_{S,γ}). r_R is only 'an integer' from Lemma 2.3.3 (any upper bound works), and even the minimal one is ⩾ 1 whenever R̄ is reducible, which the hypotheses of Prop. 2.6.6 allow (R_ℚ irreducible; Lemma 2.3.5(a) or (b), and (b) allows semisimple reducible R̄). The rows are available whenever θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) up to less than c: e.g. [F:F⁺] = 1, which §2.4–2.6 allow, where Lemma 2.6.4 holds, with θ_S surjective. So the first part is false as stated. It is TRUE when 𝔣(r)r_R = 0: abundance then means A invertible, and C = A^{−1} works with exponent m − m₀. It is also trivially true for r = 1. The second part is derived from the first. Versions: v1/v2 have no Prop. 2.6.7; the same inference is in the proof of the rank-one theorem ('By the definition of a (S,γ)-abundant pair, we may choose a basis…'). v3 is identical to the published text. Independent check 2: Quote checked on the page image, p. 135 (PDF 29): 'For every (S, γ)-abundant r-tuple … one can choose a basis …', and 'Proof The first part is obvious from Definition 2.6.5.' Definitions checked: exp_λ(x,M) = min{d : λ^d x = 0} (Def. 2.1.6, p. 123); abundance (Def. 2.6.5, p. 134). Set n = m − m₀ and identify Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) with row vectors over O_λ/λ^n. Then abundance says exactly that the matrix A = (θ_S(Ψ_i)(s_j)) satisfies im A ⊇ λ^c(O_λ/λ^n)^r, with c = 𝔣(r)𝔯_R. The claimed basis exists iff AC is diagonal for some C ∈ GL_r. Column operations preserve im A, and the image of a diagonal matrix is the product of its coordinate projections. Counterexample. Take A = [[λ,1],[0,λ]] with n ≥ 2. Its image {(λx+y, λy)} contains λ²(O_λ/λ^n)² and has index |k|². Its projections have indices 1 and |k|, so no diagonalizing basis exists. A is abundant once c ≥ 2, i.e. r ≥ 2 and 𝔯_R ≥ 1. Arithmetic realization, with [F:F⁺] = 1, where Lemma 2.6.4 does hold. Take F = ℚ(√2,√5) (real, so 𝔠 acts trivially), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, and m ≥ 5. Let S be generated by κ(1+√2) and κ((1+√5)/2); these are independent modulo cubes (take norms to the two quadratic subfields), so S is free of rank 2. Take γ = 1 (h_γ = 1). Then K ≅ (ℤ/3^m)², θ_S is bijective, and G_{S,γ} = K by Chebotarev. Choose Frobenii Ψ₁, Ψ₂ with rows (3,1) and (0,3). With 𝔯_R := 1, which is a legitimate bound in the sense of Lemma 2.3.3 ('at most 𝔯_R'), the pair is abundant (λ⁴ ⊆ λ²), yet no basis diagonalizes it. If 𝔯_R is instead read as the exact depth, this R gives 𝔯_R = 0. In that case abundance forces A to be invertible and the first part holds. The statement is then false exactly when R̄ is not absolutely irreducible and θ_S(G_{S,γ}) contains the two rows, which is automatic wherever Lemma 2.6.4 holds and θ_S is onto. Versions: v3 is identical. v1 already had the same inference inside the rank-one proof. The first reading's correction (i)–(iii) is sound. Reach to the main theorems: Prop. 2.6.7 is used in Theorem 8.2.2 with r = 1, where the first part is trivially true, and in Theorem 8.3.2 with r = 2 (pp. 317–318, 320). For every λ produced by Lemma 8.1.3 (Prop. 2.7.2(2)) or Lemma 8.1.4 (Lemma 8.1.5(1)), R̄ = R̄₀⊗R̄₁ is absolutely irreducible, so r_R = 0 and Prop. 2.6.7 holds as used. Hence E2 does not affect Theorem 1.1.1 or the prime sets of Theorem 1.1.7 and its rank-one analogue. For a general admissible λ, Definition 8.1.1 requires irreducibility of R_ℚ only in characteristic 0 ((L3)), so R̄ may be reducible and r_R ⩾ 1. The proof of Theorem 8.3.2 (Theorem 1.1.9) must then choose the abundant pair suitably, or use a one-sided variant, instead of 'fixing' an arbitrary one. That is a local repair, available whenever a correct Prop. 2.6.6 is (which E1 undermines only when R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠). E2 alone makes no main theorem false and leaves only a minor gap in the proof of Theorem 1.1.9. Only Theorem 8.3.2 uses the first part with r = 2; it underlies Theorem 1.1.9 and the unstated rank-one analogue of 1.1.7. Theorem 8.2.2 uses Proposition 2.6.7 with r = 1, where the first part is trivially true, so Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5 and 1.1.7 are untouched by E2. The failure needs 𝔯_R ≥ 1, i.e. R̄ = R̄₀⊗R̄₁ not absolutely irreducible. Definition 8.1.1 allows this: (L3) is a characteristic-0 condition, (L4) concerns the factors, and (L5-1)(b) allows a semisimple reducible R̄. For such admissible λ the proof of 8.3.2 cites a false statement. Repair where G_{S,γ} is known. Take s₁ := λ₀^{m−m_per}s, which is primitive by footnote 33, so a₁ = 1. Extend it to a basis {s₁,s₂}. Then pick Ψ₁, Ψ₂ with θ_S(Ψ₁) = λ^c s₁* and θ_S(Ψ₂) = λ^c s₂*. This is immediate if θ_S(G_{S,γ}) = θ_S(K) ∩ Hom(S,(R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ}) and O_λ = ℤ_ℓ; otherwise it needs a short argument about O_λ-spans versus subgroups. Constants (8.11)–(8.13) change harmlessly. The repair presupposes the description of G_{S,γ} that E1 removes when R_ℚ ≅ R_ℚ^𝔠, so E2 and E1 must be repaired together. E2 by itself does not put Theorem 1.1.9 in doubt, and no main theorem is shown false. The same mistake at Proof of Theorem 8.3.2, (8.11), published pp. 317–318: The diagonal basis comes from Proposition 2.6.7, which does not follow from Definition 2.6.5 for r = 2 (E2): the abundant pair with rows λ^{m_Σ}(λ, 1), λ^{m_Σ}(0, λ) (abundant once 4𝔯_R ⩾ 2) admits no such basis. But the proof uses only loc_{w1}(s2) = 0, exp loc_{w2}(s2) ⩾ m − m_Σ − 4𝔯_R and exp loc_{w1}(s) ⩾ m − m_per − 4𝔯_R. These follow from abundance directly: the matrix A′ = λ^{−m_Σ}(θ_S(Ψ_i)(e_j)) over O_λ/λ^{m−m_Σ} has elementary divisors dividing λ^{4𝔯_R}, so A′v has a coordinate of valuation ⩽ 4𝔯_R for every primitive v; and a primitive t spanning the kernel of the unimodular part of the first row has θ_S(Ψ1)(t) = 0 with A′t, hence θ_S(Ψ2)(t), of valuation ⩽ 4𝔯_R. So the threshold m > m_per + m_lat + m_Σ + 8𝔯_R + m_dif is unchanged. For r = 1 (Theorem 8.2.2) Proposition 2.6.7 is correct.

sourceIssues.printed: The source chooses a positive integer e_α such that the order of (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{e_α}} is coprime to ℓ and h_{(γ′_α)^{ℓ^{e_α}}} has eigenvalue 1. It then replaces γ′_α with (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{d_α e_α}} and claims to obtain the required (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′).
sourceIssues.correction: Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) whose image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) mod λ^m lifts (γ₀, γ₁, ξ), and replace g by g^{ℓ^k} for ONE k that kills the ℓ-parts (the kernel of reduction mod λ is an ℓ-group) and is divisible by the d_α and by the order of Frobenius on the residue fields involved; then (γ′₀^{ℓ^k}, γ′₁^{ℓ^k}, ξ′^{ℓ^k}) lies in the image, reduces to (γ₀, γ₁, ξ) and satisfies (a)–(e). For (c) one needs ker(h − 1) free of rank one over O_λ/λ^m, not only '1 is an eigenvalue': this follows since h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent, a free direct summand lifting the rank-one residual kernel.
sourceIssues.reason: Choosing powers independently in the two representations need not give an element in the image of the same Galois element. A common power preserves joint-image membership, the residual triple and the required unit conditions. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — checked on the page image of p. 136; the triple obtained by independent ℓ-powers of γ′₀, γ′₁ with ξ′ unchanged need not be in the image of the joint homomorphism. Minor and easily repaired; the lemma is true. The previous record's 'printed' field did not quote the faulty step (corrected below). (GI^m) asks for a single element of the image of Gal(F̄/F′) under the joint map (ρ̄₀₊^{(m)}, ρ̄₁₊^{(m)}, ε̄_ℓ^{(m)}). Powers of the components by different exponents ℓ^{d₀e₀} ≠ ℓ^{d₁e₁}, with ξ′ unchanged, correspond to different Galois elements. Defence: the intended argument is obviously the common power (as in arXiv v1/v2), and conditions (a), (d), (e) are Galois-stable (𝒫 ∈ ℤ[T]; eigenvalue conditions invariant under x ↦ x^{ℓ^k}), so nothing beyond the proof is affected. Independent check: Quote checked on the image of p. 136: 'Replacing γ′_α by (γ′_α)^{ℓ^{d_α e_α}}, we obtain the desired element (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′).' (GI^m_{F′,𝒫}) asks for ONE element of the image of Gal(F̄/F′) under the joint map (ρ̄₀₊^{(m)}, ρ̄₁₊^{(m)}, ε̄_ℓ^{(m)}). Powering the two components by different exponents ℓ^{d₀e₀}, ℓ^{d₁e₁} and keeping ξ′ gives a triple that in general comes from no single Galois element. The repair is routine. Take g ∈ Gal(F̄/F′) with image (γ′₀, γ′₁, ξ′) lifting (γ₀, γ₁, ξ). Replace g by g^{ℓ^k} with k divisible by d₀, d₁ and by [O_λ/λ : 𝔽_ℓ], and large enough to kill the ℓ-part: the kernel of 𝒢(O_λ/λ^m) → 𝒢(O_λ/λ) is an ℓ-group, and ℓ^k is odd, so the c-component is preserved. The reduction is unchanged, so (a), (d) and (e), which only depend on it, persist; (b) holds by construction. For (c), h has order prime to ℓ, so ker(h−1) is the image of the averaging idempotent: a free direct summand whose rank is the residual multiplicity 1. The printed phrase '1 is an eigenvalue' does not give (c) by itself. Versions: v1 (Lemma 2.6.1, '(3) implies (2)') says 'after raising sufficiently large ℓ-power, (γ′0, γ′1, ξ′) will satisfy (2a)–(2e)', a common power; v3 is identical to print.

sourceIssues.locator: Construction 3.1.8(1) and (2), published pp. 141–142; arXiv v3 p. 24; v1 p. 24
sourceIssues.printed: In (1), the source arranges the entries of α in the sequence (α1, . . . , αN), requiring αiαN+1−i = 1, and claims a unique homomorphism. In (2), its chosen sequences for α1 and α2 are respectively (α1,1, . . . , α1,N) and (α2,1, . . . , α2,N), subject to α1,iα2,N+1−i = 1.
sourceIssues.correction: Either assume L is an integral domain (then unitarity makes the multisets inverse-stable and the orderings exist), or define φ_α from P_α alone: for N even write P_α(T) = T^{N/2}Q(T + T^{−1}) (for N odd first divide by T − 1, which divides P_α since unitarity forces P_α(1) = 0) and send the i-th elementary symmetric function of x_j + x_j^{−1} in ℤ[X_*(A_{N,v})]^W to the corresponding signed coefficient of Q; similarly in the split case.
sourceIssues.reason: In L=F5×F5 use the three roots (1,2),(2,1),(3,3). Componentwise the polynomial is (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), which has the required odd reciprocal identity. No root has square one in L, so no root can occupy the middle of a reciprocal ordering. This does not obstruct the usual field-valued construction. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): revised: the gap is real (the counterexample checks) and occurs also in the split case (2), but every use of Construction 3.1.8 is over ℂ or with an ordered tuple given, so it affects nothing (previous record: 'the proof'). Inert case (previous record, rechecked): L = 𝔽_5 × 𝔽_5, α = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,3)}: both components give (T−1)(T−2)(T−3) = T³ + 4T² + T + 4 over 𝔽_5, which equals (−T)³P(T^{−1}) because 2·3 = 1; but no element squares to 1 (so none can be the middle entry) and (1,2)(2,1) = (2,2) ≠ 1. Split case (new): L = 𝔽_5 × 𝔽_5, α_1 = {(1,2), (2,1)}, α_2 = {(1,1), (3,3)}: P_{α_1} = (T−1)(T−2) and T²P_{α_2}(T^{−1}) = (1−T)(1−3T) = 3(T−1)(T−2) over 𝔽_5, so α is unitary with c = 2; the inverses (1,3), (3,1) of the elements of α_1 do not lie in α_2, so no orders with α_{1,i}α_{2,N+1−i} = 1 exist. Defence: over a field or domain the orderings exist, and when they exist the value of φ_α is independent of the choice (valid orderings give Weyl-conjugate characters). The construction is used only in Construction 3.1.10 with L = ℂ, and Notation B.2.5 starts from an ordered tuple. Independent check: Construction 3.1.8 (pp. 141–142) and Definition 3.1.3 (p. 139) were checked on the images: L is an arbitrary ℤ[‖v‖^{±δ(v)/2}]-ring. Both counterexamples recomputed over 𝔽₅×𝔽₅. Inert case: each component of P_α is (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), and (−T)³P(T^{−1}) = (T−1)(T−2)(T−3), so α is unitary. No element squares to (1,1), and (1,2)(2,1) = (2,2), so no admissible ordering exists. Split case: P_{α₁} = (T−1)(T−2), and T²P_{α₂}(T^{−1}) = (1−T)(1−3T) = 3(T−1)(T−2), so α is unitary with c = 2. But (1,3) and (3,1) are not in α₂, so no ordering with α_{1,i}α_{2,N+1−i} = 1 exists. Over a domain the multisets are inversion-stable and orderings exist. When orderings exist, φ_α is independent of the choice: inverses in a ring are unique, so two orderings differ by a Weyl element. The construction is used only with L = ℂ: Construction 3.1.10, and Definition 6.1.8 via φ_{α(BC(π_v))}. Notation B.2.5 starts from an ordered tuple. The first reading's alternative is also sound over any ring: for N odd, a_i = −a_{N−i} forces P_α(1) = 0 without inverting 2. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

DL(V, { , }, 1) is the set of lines with x_1^4 + t x_2^4 = 0: four geometric points, none F_9-rational because the fourth powers in F_9^× are {±1} = F_3^× (computer count: 0 rational points for each of the six t ∉ F_3, 4 for t ∈ F_3^×). Frobenius therefore permutes H^0 = L^4 non-trivially (L = Q_5 is 3-coprime with p + 1 = 4 invertible). N = 4: for p = 2, κ = F_4, the split form gives #DL(V, 3)(F_4) = (q²+1)(q³+1) = 45 = 1 + 4·7 + 16 (Frobenius acts trivially on H^2(1); b_2 = 7 for the Hermitian cubic surface), whereas random non-degenerate forms over F_4 (all admissible) give 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29 or 33 points, so trace(Frob | H^2(1)) = (# − 17)/4 ≠ 7 and the action is non-trivial. The cited fact (‘spanned by Tate cycles over κ’) is true only when the relevant cycles are defined over κ, i.e. for the split form. Independent check: Checked on pp. 322–323. The lemma is stated for any pair over any κ ⊇ F_{p²} with dim 𝒱^⊣ = 0; it does not even assume admissibility, which holds anyway by Lang. The proof says 'The lemma is trivial if N = 2' and '…is spanned by Tate cycles over κ ([31])'. Re-derived. For N = 2, κ = F_9, {x,y} = x1^σy1 + t x2^σy2, the isotropic points satisfy u^4 = −t. A computer count gives 0 F_9-rational points for each of the six t ∉ F_3 and 4 for t ∈ F_3^×. Frobenius therefore permutes H^0 = L^4 non-trivially, e.g. for L = Q_5 (3-coprime, p+1 invertible). For N = 4, p = 2, κ = F_4, the cubic surface {y,y} = 0 has 45 = 1 + 4·7 + 16 points for the split (Hermitian) form. Random non-degenerate forms give 9, 13, 17, 21, 25, 29 or 33 points, so tr(Frob | H^2(1)) ≠ 7 and the action is not trivial. The cited fact is true only when the Tate classes (F_{p²}-rational linear subspaces) are defined over κ, i.e. for κ-forms that are split. The only use is Lemma 5.6.2(3) (p. 212), whose proof is complete except for (4): the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius defines an F_p^Φ-form of each fibre. So that proof inherits a gap (E9). The needed special case, split forms, is very plausibly true, so Lemma 5.6.2(3) and everything downstream stand. The same mistake at Proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3), published p. 212 (relies on Lemma A.1.4(4), p. 323: Lemma A.1.4(4) asserts that Gal(κ̄/κ) acts trivially on H^{N−2}(DL(𝒱, {,}, N−1)_{κ̄}, L((N−2)/2)) for EVERY pair over κ with 𝒱^⊣ = 0. Admissibility (Definition A.1.1) only provides an 𝔽_{p²}-structure over κ̄, and the claim is false in general. E9's example, re-checked here: κ = 𝔽₉, p = 3, N = 2, {x, y} = x₁^σy₁ + t x₂^σy₂ with t ∉ 𝔽₃. The isotropic points u⁴ = −t are not 𝔽₉-rational, and Frob₉ multiplies u by t² ≠ 1. The 𝔽_{p²}-structure is the fixed space of Φ = 𝔽𝕍⁻¹; here Φ acts on 𝒱 as diag(−1, −t²), not as a scalar. The proof of Lemma 5.6.2(3) invokes exactly this false generality. Construction 5.3.6 only shows that Frobenius preserves Sh(V°, K°_p), i.e. each fibre up to 𝔗; it says nothing about the κ-structure of the fibre. Defence: for the Shimura fibres, Φ^{[κ:𝔽_{p²}]} is the scalar π_{A°}/p^k = τ_∞^c(π_{A₀}/p^k), a root of unity, which acts trivially on ℙ(𝒱_{s°}). So the κ-structure agrees with the 𝔽_{p²}-structure, and Lemma 5.6.2(3) is very plausibly true. The paper does not supply this argument. Lemma 5.6.2(3) is used in Lemma 5.9.3(6) and §6. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 212: 'Part (3) follows from Lemma A.1.4(4) and Construction 5.3.6.' Construction 5.3.6 (p. 199) says only that Gal(F̄_p/F_p^Φ) acts trivially on Sh(V°, −K°_p) under υ°, and through 𝔗 on T_p. So on the 𝔗-invariant cohomology (Notation 3.5.7) the 𝔗-twisted Frobenius stabilises each link fibre DL_{s°}. Prime-to-p quasi-isogenies identify Dieudonné modules, so this twisted Frobenius acts on V_{s°} ⊗ F̄_p by a σ^f-semilinear bijection that preserves { , }_{s°} up to a scalar. In other words it is the Frobenius of an F_p^Φ-form of a non-degenerate pair. Lemma A.1.4(4), as stated, would then finish the proof. So the proof is complete except for A.1.4(4), which is false in that generality: see E9, whose N = 2 case (F_9) and N = 4 case (F_4: split form 45 points, random non-degenerate forms 9–33 points) I re-ran by computer. What is missing is exactly the check that the forms arising are split, i.e. that the twisted Frobenius is a scalar times a power of the F_{p²}-Frobenius. That holds via η°_𝔭 (Construction 5.6.1) or π_{A°} = i(π_{A0}), and the paper does not give it. So the gap is real and Lemma 5.6.2(3) is very likely true. It is still the same mistake as E9. A.1.4(4) is used only here (grep: its only citation is p. 212). The authors' route is 'A.1.4(4) holds for every κ-form', and restricting A.1.4(4) to split forms (E9's correction) forces precisely the verification this record supplies. Uses of Lemma 5.6.2(3): Lemma 5.9.3(6) (p. 235), Lemma 7.2.5(4) (p. 291), §6.

sourceIssues.printed: The source places ℙ(Y_N) inside Iso(Λ̄_N), yielding a class in CH^{r−1}(Iso(Λ̄_N)). It claims that subtracting c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)_κ̄}(1)) from its cohomology class gives a nonzero element of H^prim(Iso(Λ̄_N)_κ̄, Q̄_ℓ)(r−1).
sourceIssues.correction: Replace 'its cohomology class subtracted by c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)_κ̄}(1))' with '[ℙ(Y_N)] − (q+1)^{−1}·c_1(O_{ℙ(Λ̄_N)_κ̄}(1))^{r−1}' for r ⩾ 2. For r = 1, use [pt] − (q+1)^{−1}·1 in the reduced H^0; see E10 for the definition of H^prim when N = 2.
sourceIssues.reason: The linear cycle has codimension r−1, so subtracting a degree-two class is wrong for r≠2. Its pairing with the complementary hyperplane power is one, whereas the hypersurface hyperplane top degree is q+1; this gives the normalization even at r=2. Page image checked. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed (published label: proof of Proposition C.2.1(2), p. 355). ℙ(Y_N) ≅ ℙ^{r−1} has codimension r−1 in the (2r−2)-dimensional Iso(Λ̄_N), so its class lies in H^{2r−2}(r−1) while c_1(O(1)) lies in H^2(1): the subtraction is degree-inconsistent unless r = 2. H^{2r}(Iso) is spanned by h^r, and ∪h kills [ℙ(Y_N)] − c·h^{r−1} iff c = ([ℙ(Y_N)]·h^{r−1})/(h^{2r−2}) = deg ℙ^{r−1}/deg Iso = 1/(q+1). Even for r = 2 the coefficient is 1/(q+1), not 1. The 'well-known' nonvanishing is true: if [ℙ(Y_N)] = h^{r−1}/(q+1) then [ℙ(Y_N)]^2 = 1/(q+1), whereas the self-intersection is c_{r−1}(N_{ℙ(Y_N)/Iso}) = ((−q)^r − 1)/(−(q+1)) ∈ ℤ (from c(N) = (1+h)^r/(1+(q+1)h)). Defence: 'subtracted by c_1(…)' can be read loosely as 'minus the appropriate multiple of the appropriate power of the hyperplane class'; the conclusion Ω^{P^{(r)}} ≠ 0 is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked; the passage runs from the last line of p. 354 onto p. 355. H^prim is defined on p. 353 as ker(∪c_1(O(1)): H^{N−2} → H^N(1)). ℙ(Y_N) ≅ ℙ^{r−1} has codimension r−1 in the (2r−2)-dimensional Fermat hypersurface Iso(Λ̄_N), which has degree q+1. So its class lies in H^{2r−2}(r−1), and subtracting c_1 ∈ H^2(1) is degree-inconsistent for r ≠ 2. Even for r = 2 it is wrong: ([ℙ^1] − h)·h = 1 − (q+1) ≠ 0. H^{2r}(Iso) is spanned by h^r, so [ℙ(Y_N)] − c·h^{r−1} is primitive iff 1 − c(q+1) = 0, i.e. c = 1/(q+1). The difference is nonzero: [ℙ(Y_N)]² = c_{r−1}(N_{ℙ(Y_N)/Iso}) = ((−q)^r − 1)/(−(q+1)) ∈ ℤ, while (h^{r−1}/(q+1))² = 1/(q+1) ∉ ℤ. I rechecked this Chern-class computation from c(N) = (1+h)^r/(1+(q+1)h). The first reading's mathematics is right. But the intended meaning (subtract the multiple of h^{r−1} that projects onto the primitive part) is clear, and the conclusion Ω_N^{P^{(r)}} ≠ 0 stands once the formula is corrected. Following the convention for misprints whose correction leaves the argument intact, 'affects' should be 'nothing', not 'the proof'. Versions: identical in v1/v2/v3 p. 165.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Lemma 8.1.7, published p. 307; arXiv v3 Lemma 8.1.7, PDF p. 134; arXiv v1/v2 Lemma 8.1.4, PDF p. 133
sourceIssues.printed: The source invokes torsion freeness over O_λ of H^i_ét(Sh(V_{n1}, K^𝔓_{n1}K′^𝔭_{n1,𝔓}K^?_{n1,𝔭})_{F̄}, O_λ)_{𝔪1} for all i ∈ ℤ. It then reduces the task to proving (8.1), an isomorphism of the corresponding groups after ⊗_{O_λ} ℚ̄_ℓ, as ℚ̄_ℓ[Γ_F]-modules for all i ∈ ℤ.
sourceIssues.correction: Show that the Hecke correspondence T^{•∘}_{n1,𝔭}: H^i(Sh(…K°_{n1,𝔭}), O_λ)_{𝔪1} → H^i(Sh(…K•_{n1,𝔭}), O_λ)_{𝔪1} (integral, Γ_F- and prime-to-𝔓-Hecke-equivariant) is an isomorphism. By the printed local computation, T^{∘•}∘T^{•∘} acts on the π1-part of the source by c(π1) = p^{r1²+r1}∏_{i=1}^{r1}(α_i+p)(α_i+p^{−1})/α_i (Proposition B.4.3(1)), and T^{•∘}∘T^{∘•} acts on the π1-part of the target by the same scalar (one-dimensional K°- and K•-invariants of the same constituent). Since the Satake parameter of BC(π1)_𝔭 is congruent mod λ to that of Π_{1,𝔭}, intertwining genericity mod λ (which presupposes p invertible mod λ) makes every c(π1) a λ-adic unit; hence both composites have unit determinant on the free O_λ-modules H^i(…)_{𝔪1}, are automorphisms, and T^{•∘} is an O_λ[Γ_F]-isomorphism (also 𝕋^{Σ⁺_min∪Σ⁺_𝔓}-linear).
sourceIssues.reason: Freeness of source and target and a rational isomorphism do not imply an integral isomorphism: multiplication by λ on Oλ is a counterexample. P5 and the explicit compositions offer the missing integrality input; the full uniform construction remains to be written. Re-checked on the page image (2026-09-23): confirmed — locator corrected (it is Lemma 8.1.7, not a Proposition) and the correction sharpened to an explicit determinant argument using only the paper's own inputs. Torsion-free O_λ[Γ_F]-modules with isomorphic rationalizations need not be isomorphic: Γ = ℤ acting on O_λ² by (1 1; 0 1) and by (1 λ; 0 1) gives rationally conjugate, integrally non-isomorphic lattices (their reductions mod λ are a nontrivial unipotent and the identity). The integral statement is essential: in (8.7) and its rank-one analogue it transports the fixed exponent m_lat, defined at hyperspecial level, to the level-raised Shimura variety at a prime 𝔭 that depends on m; with only a rational isomorphism the lattice discrepancy could grow with 𝔭 and the final choice 'm > m_per + m_lat + …' would be circular. Case for the defence: every ingredient of the repair (the integral correspondences of Definition 5.8.1, Proposition B.4.3(1), intertwining genericity mod λ) is already in the printed proof; only the passage from 'nonzero' to 'unit' and the determinant argument are missing, so the lemma as stated is true. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 307. The inference 'torsion-free, and isomorphic after ⊗Q̄_ℓ, hence isomorphic as O_λ[Γ_F]-modules' is invalid in general; the first reading's unipotent example is correct. It is not rescued in this setting. If H^{2r₁}_{𝔪₁} ⊗ Q̄_ℓ were isotypic for one residually absolutely irreducible ρ, every Γ-stable lattice would be ≅ T^{⊕μ} (O_λ[Γ] ↠ End(T) by Burnside and Nakayama, then Morita). But localization at 𝔪₁ only fixes the residual eigensystem, so several π₁ with distinct ρ_{BC(π₁)} lifting ρ̄ can contribute, and lattices in such a sum need not be isomorphic. The repair works, and I checked it. I° = T^{∘•}T^{•∘} ∈ 𝕋°_{𝔭} acts on each π₁-part by a scalar that is, up to a power of p, ∏(p + α_i)(p + α_i^{-1}) = P(−p)/(−(p + 1)). Its value for π₁ is congruent mod λ to its value for Π₁ (Chebotarev), and it is a unit because P_{α(Π_{1,𝔭})}(−p) is invertible mod λ (Definition 3.1.5(2)). The same scalar governs T^{•∘}T^{∘•} on the one-dimensional K•-invariants. Hence both composites have unit determinant on the free modules H^i_{𝔪₁}, and the integral, Γ_F- and Hecke-equivariant T^{•∘} is an isomorphism. The lemma is true; the integral statement is essential for the m_lat bookkeeping in (8.7).

It views G^i/G^{i+1} as an 𝔽_ℓ[G]-submodule of End(R̄), and thus (G^i/G^{i+1}) ⊗ O_λ/λ as a submodule over (O_λ/λ)[G] inside End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) ≃ End(R̄)^d, with d := [O_λ/λ : 𝔽_ℓ].
sourceIssues.correction: As (O_λ/λ)[G]-modules, End(R̄) ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≃ ⊕_{σ ∈ Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ)} End(R̄)^{(σ)} (Frobenius twists), k = O_λ/λ, not End(R̄)^d. Replace the last hypothesis of (b) by Hom_{𝔽_ℓ[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0, equivalently Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄)^{(σ)}, R̄) = 0 for every σ ∈ Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ); then the printed proof goes through. As printed, (b) is correct when k = 𝔽_ℓ.
sourceIssues.reason: Counterexample with k = 𝔽₂₅, ℓ = 5, m = 2, O_λ = W(𝔽₂₅). Let ζ generate 𝔽₂₅^× (order 24), H = ⟨h⟩ ≅ ℤ/24 acting on k² by χ₁ ⊕ χ₂, χ₁(h) = ζ⁵, χ₂(h) = ζ⁴, and G := A ⋊ H ⊆ GL₂(O_λ/25) with H = {diag([ζ⁵]^t, [ζ⁴]^t)} (Teichmüller lifts) and A = {1 + 5x·e₁₂ : x ∈ 𝔽₂₅} ≅ 𝔽₂₅, on which h acts by ψ = χ₁χ₂^{−1} (ζ). Realize G as Gal(L/F) with 5 unramified in F (any finite group is a Galois group over some number field; choose the S_n-extension of ℚ split at 5), R = (O_λ/25)². Hypotheses of (b): dim R̄ = 2 ⩽ min{3, 2}; R̄ = χ₁ ⊕ χ₂ is semisimple (A acts trivially, |H| prime to 5); End(R̄) = 1 ⊕ 1 ⊕ ψ ⊕ ψ^{−1}, exponents {0,0,1,23} versus R̄ = {5,4}, so Hom_{k[Γ_F]}(End(R̄), R̄) = 0. But the 𝔽₅-linear map A → R̄, x ↦ (x⁵, 0) is H-equivariant (ψ⁵ = χ₁), so H¹(G, R̄) ≅ Hom_H(A, R̄) ≠ 0; since R̄^G = 0, H¹(G, λR) ≅ H¹(G, R̄) injects into H¹(G, R) = ker Res_ρ. So Res_ρ is not injective. (Here (a) fails: no nontrivial scalar in the image.) Defence: the only verification of (b) in the paper (Lemma 8.1.4 via Lemma 8.1.5(2), for Theorem 1.1.7) proves via Jordan types that ρ̄₀⊗ρ̄₁ is not a subquotient of ad(ρ̄₀⊗ρ̄₁); the same argument applies to every Frobenius twist, so Theorem 1.1.7 is not affected; Theorem 1.1.1 uses (a) (Proposition 2.7.2(1)). But Definition 8.1.1 (L5-1) admits primes satisfying only (b), so Theorems 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 as stated rely on the false lemma when O_λ/λ ≠ 𝔽_ℓ. Independent check: Statement and proof checked on the images of pp. 127–128, including 'End(R̄) ⊗ (O_λ/λ) ≃ End(R̄)^d'. G^i/G^{i+1} is only an 𝔽_ℓ-subspace of End_k(R̄), with k = O_λ/λ. As k[G]-modules, End(R̄) ⊗_{𝔽_ℓ} k ≅ ⊕_{σ∈Gal(k/𝔽_ℓ)} End(R̄)^{(σ)}, which is not End(R̄)^d unless every Frobenius twist is isomorphic to End(R̄). I verified the 𝔽₂₅ counterexample by explicit computation. I built G = ⟨diag([ζ]⁵,[ζ]⁴), 1+5e₁₂⟩ ⊂ GL₂(W₂(𝔽₂₅)) with W₂(𝔽₂₅) = (ℤ/25)[√2]; it has order 600 = |A ⋊ H|. A cocycle computation over 𝔽₅ gives dim_{𝔽₅} Z¹(G,R̄) = 6, R̄^G = 0 and dim B¹ = 4, so dim_{𝔽₅} H¹(G,R̄) = 2 = dim_k Hom_H(A,R̄). As characters of h: End(R̄) = ζ^{0,0,1,23} and R̄ = ζ^{5,4}, so Hom_{k[G]}(End R̄, R̄) = 0. The Frobenius twist is ζ^{0,0,5,19} ∋ ζ⁵ = χ₁. The hypotheses of (b) hold: dim 2 ⩽ min{3, 2}, and R̄ is semisimple. Since R̄^G = 0, H¹(G,λR) ≅ H¹(G,R̄) injects into H¹(G,R) = ker Res_ρ. Realizing G as Gal(L/F) inside an S_n-extension is standard. So Lemma 2.3.5(b) is false whenever O_λ/λ ≠ 𝔽_ℓ is allowed. Reach: (L5-1) (p. 303) accepts assumption (b). Proposition 2.6.6 uses it via 'By Lemma 2.3.5, Res is injective', and so do the proofs of Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 (p. 310: 'By (L5-1) and Lemma 2.3.4'). Theorems 1.1.5/1.1.9 are therefore unproved for admissible λ with residue degree > 1 that satisfy only (b). Theorem 1.1.7 is safe: Lemma 8.1.5(2)'s Jordan-type argument works for ad(ρ)^{(σ)}, since twisting keeps the unipotent Jordan type and semisimplicity. Theorem 1.1.1 uses (a) through Proposition 2.7.2(1). Versions: identical in v1/v2 (Lemma 2.3.4) and v3.

sourceIssues.reason: Consequence of E1: in the example of E1 (F = ℚ(√5, i), ℓ = 3, R = ℤ₃(1), j = 2, S the Kummer class of u = (1+√5)/2 mod 3^m, γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠)) all four hypotheses hold (R_ℚ of rank one; −1 is a nontrivial scalar in the image of Γ_F in GL(R̄) = 𝔽₃^×; γ has order 2; (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = R̄^{(m)} free of rank one), r_S = 1, m₀ = 0, and G_{S,γ} = {1}, so θ¹_{S,γ}(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ} and no tuple is abundant once m > 𝔣(1)r_R = r_R (r_R = 0 is admissible here since R has rank one). The printed proof is fine except for its appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Independent check 1: Quotation checked on p. 134 (PDF p. 28): Prop. 2.6.6 asserts an (S,γ)-abundant r_S-tuple exists under: R_ℚ absolutely irreducible; Lemma 2.3.5(a) or (b); order of γ prime to ℓ; (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} free of rank 1. The proof (p. 135) derives this from Lemma 2.6.4. The example of E1 satisfies every hypothesis (see E1 for the §2.1–2.6 conventions): R_ℚ = ℚ₃(1) has rank one; ε̄(Γ_F) = 𝔽₃^× contains the nontrivial scalar −1; γ = ρ̄₊^{(m)}(𝔠) has order 2; h_γ = 1, so (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} = μ_{3^m} is free of rank 1; S = ℤ/3^m·κ(u) has m₀ = 0 and r_S = 1. Recomputed G_{S,γ} = {1}, so θ¹_{S,γ}(Ψ) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}. Its image cannot contain λ^{𝔣(1)r_R}Hom(S, R̄^{(m)}) ≠ 0 once m > r_R, and r_R depends only on R (r_R = 0 is admissible here). So the proposition is false for all large m. The proof's only faulty step is the appeal to Lemma 2.6.4. Instances inside the paper's own setting also exist. Take R = R₊|_{Γ_F}. If S lies in the ε-eigenspace and γ acts on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} ⊂ R̄₊ by −ε, then loc_w(S) = 0 at every γ-associated place and no abundant element exists. If r_S = 2 and S = S₊ ⊕ S₋ meets both eigenspaces, then for every γ one summand is killed by all Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}, so no γ admits an abundant pair. sourceIssues.printed: For an odd rational prime ℓ unramified in F, the source sets R_α := (Sym^{n_α−1}_{ℤ_ℓ} H¹_ét(A_{αF̄}, ℤ_ℓ))(r_α) for α = 0, 1, regarding it as a ℤ_ℓ[Γ_F]-module. It asserts that R_α has rank n_α in Mod(F, ℤ_ℓ)_fr and carries the canonical polarization Ξ_α: R_α^𝔠 ⥲ R_α^∨(1 − α), of type (1 − α).
sourceIssues.correction: Require ℓ ⩾ n_α (sufficient; then all C(n_α−1, a) are ℓ-units), e.g. 'for ℓ > n₁'.
sourceIssues.reason: The polarization is induced from the Weil pairing on H¹ (a perfect alternating pairing on a rank-two lattice T); on Sym^k T the induced pairing pairs x^a y^{k−a} with x^{k−a}y^a by ±a!(k−a)! (or ±1/binom(k,a) if normalized), which is not a unit when ℓ ⩽ k = n_α − 1. Then Sym^k T and its dual (a divided-power lattice) are not homothetic Galois lattices when the image is large (e.g. ℓ = 3, n_α ⩾ 4), so no (1−α)-polarization of R_α exists. Defence: only large ℓ are used. Independent check: Text checked on the images of pp. 136–137: 'For a rational prime ℓ (that is odd and unramified in F) … R_α is an object in Mod(F, ℤ_ℓ)_fr of rank n_α with a canonical (1 − α)-polarization'. A_α is defined over F⁺, so R_α^𝔠 ≅ R_α. A (1−α)-polarization therefore amounts to Sym^k H¹ ≅ Γ^k H¹ as Γ_F-lattices, where k = n_α − 1; the twists match via the Weil pairing. Both are lattices in Sym^k V. For non-CM A_α the image of Γ_F is open in GL₂(ℤ_ℓ), so Sym^k V is absolutely irreducible, and an isomorphism would have to be a homothety. With the basis x^a y^{k−a}, the natural map to the divided powers is multiplication by a!(k−a)!. So the lattices are homothetic iff every binomial coefficient C(k,a) is prime to ℓ. That holds for k < ℓ and fails for ℓ ⩽ k ⩽ 2ℓ−2; examples are ℓ = 3 with n₀ = 4 (C(3,1) = 3) or n₁ = 5 (C(4,2) = 6). The first reading's 'ℓ = 3, n_α ⩾ 4' is slightly too broad. For n_α = 6 every C(5,a) is prime to 3, so a polarization exists; the same happens whenever k = dℓ^e − 1. Only large ℓ are used (Proposition 2.7.2, Lemma 8.1.3). Versions: same text in v1 and v3.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 3.1.6(2),(3), published p. 140; arXiv v3 p. 24; v1 p. 23
sourceIssues.printed: The source interprets (2) as excluding the pair {−‖v‖, −‖v‖−1} from α, and (3) as requiring precisely one occurrence of {‖v‖, ‖v‖−1} in α.
sourceIssues.correction: Add the hypothesis ‖v‖² ≠ 1 in L (for (2) it is enough that ‖v‖ ≠ −1 in L).
sourceIssues.reason: Let L be a field with char L ≠ 2 and P = P_α unitary. Write P = (T−1)^k R with R(1) ≠ 0. The identity P(T) = (−T)^N P(T^{−1}) gives R(1) = (−1)^{N+k}R(1), so k ≡ N (mod 2); likewise the multiplicity of −1 is even. (3) If ‖v‖ = 1 in L (N even), then 'P(‖v‖) = 0 and P′(‖v‖) invertible' would make 1 a simple root, which is impossible. Yet the pair {1, 1} can appear exactly once: for example ‖v‖ = 7, L = 𝔽_3, N = 2, α = {1, 1}. (2) If ‖v‖ = −1 in L (N odd), then P(−‖v‖) = P(1) = 0 always, so P is never intertwining generic. Yet the pair {1, 1} can be absent: for example N = 1, α = {1}. (1), (4) and the last sentence of the remark are correct. Defence: the remark is an 'easy to see' aside. In every use ‖v‖² ≠ 1 in L: (P2)/(PI2) require ℓ ∤ p(p² − 1) for L = O_E/λ, and Proposition C.2.5 works over ℂ. Independent check: Remark 3.1.6 checked on the image of p. 140. For unitary P with char L ≠ 2, write P = (T∓1)^k R. The functional equation forces the multiplicity of 1 to be ≡ N (mod 2) and the multiplicity of −1 to be even. (3): if ‖v‖ = ±1 in L (N even), the root ‖v‖ always has even multiplicity. So 'P(‖v‖) = 0, P′(‖v‖) invertible' never holds, although the pair can occur exactly once; for example L = 𝔽₃, ‖v‖ = 7, α = {1,1}. (2): if ‖v‖ = −1 in L (N odd), then P(−‖v‖) = P(1) = 0 always, while the pair {1,1} can be absent; for example N = 1, α = {1}. Items (1), (4) and the last sentence are correct, and (2), (3) are correct when ‖v‖² ≠ 1. Uses: the remark is cited only in Proposition C.2.5, over ℂ with q > 1. In §§6–8, (P2)/(PI2) impose ℓ ∤ p(p²−1) with ‖𝔭‖ = p, so the case never arises. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

sourceIssues.locator: Construction 3.1.10, published p. 142; arXiv v3 p. 25; v1 p. 25
sourceIssues.printed: Under Π ∘ c ≃ Π∨, the source asserts unitarity of the Satake parameter α(Πv) whenever v ∉ Σ+Π.
sourceIssues.correction: Assume in addition that the central character ω_Π is trivial on 𝔸_{F^+}^× (true for relevant Π). In general only α(Π_v) = α(Π_v)^{−1} as multisets holds, and at an inert v the product of the entries equals ω_Π(ϖ_v) = ±1.
sourceIssues.reason: At an unramified inert v, Π_w ∘ c ≃ Π_w^∨ and c(ϖ_v) = ϖ_v give α(Π_v) = α(Π_v)^{−1} as multisets. Hence (−T)^N P_α(T^{−1}) = (∏α_i)^{−1}P_α(T) with ∏α_i = ω_{Π_w}(ϖ_v). Since ω_Π ∘ c = ω_Π^{−1}, the restriction ω_Π|_{𝔸_{F^+}^×} is quadratic and trivial on norms, so it equals 1 or η_{F/F^+}; in the second case ω(ϖ_v) = −1 and α(Π_v) is not unitary. Explicit counterexample: N = 1, Π = χ a Hecke character of 𝔸_F^×/F^× extending η_{F/F^+} (it exists by Pontryagin duality). Then χ·χ^c = η ∘ Nm = 1, so χ ∘ c = χ^{−1}, but α(χ_v) = {−1} at every inert unramified v, and T + 1 ≠ (−T)(T^{−1} + 1). Defence: the construction is used only for relevant Π. There Definition 1.1.3(3) makes the archimedean central character arg^{Σ(N+1−2i)} = 1, which is incompatible with η_{F/F^+} (the sign character at each real place), so ω_Π|_{𝔸_{F^+}^×} = 1 and the claim holds. Independent check: Construction 3.1.10 checked on the image of p. 142, with Π cuspidal on GL_N(𝔸_F) (p. 138). At an inert unramified v, c(ϖ_v) = ϖ_v and Π∘c ≃ Π^∨ give α = α^{−1} as multisets. Hence (−T)^N P_α(T^{−1}) = (∏α_i)P_α(T), and unitarity (Definition 3.1.3(1)) is equivalent to ω_Π(ϖ_v) = 1. ω_Π restricted to 𝔸_{F⁺}^× is quadratic and trivial on norms, so it is 1 or η_{F/F⁺}. The counterexample works: χ extending η_{F/F⁺} exists by Pontryagin duality and is unramified almost everywhere by continuity. It satisfies χ∘c = χ^{−1}, and α(χ_v) = {−1} is not unitary for N = 1, since that would force α = {1}. For relevant Π (Definition 1.1.3(3)), the archimedean central character is arg^{Σ(N+1−2i)} = 1. This excludes η, which is the sign character at real places, so the claim holds wherever the construction is used. Versions: same in v1 and v3.

sourceIssues.locator: Remark 3.2.6 (second sentence), published p. 145; arXiv v3 p. 27; v1 p. 27
sourceIssues.printed: The source claims that Hypothesis 3.2.10 makes Q(Π) a strong coefficient field for Π when Π ≃ BC(π) comes from a standard pair (V, π) as in Definition 3.2.7, with V standard indefinite.
sourceIssues.correction: Either add the hypothesis that ρ_{Π,ι_ℓ} is irreducible for every ι_ℓ and give the descent argument, or delete the sentence. It is never used: all results take a strong coefficient field E as given, and one exists by [16, Proposition 3.2.5].
sourceIssues.reason: Hypothesis 3.2.10 only says something when ρ_{BC(π),ι_ℓ} is irreducible, which the remark does not assume and which is not known in general for relevant Π. Even granting irreducibility, the natural Q(Π)_λ-rational object is the φ_Π-eigenpart M of H^{N−1}_ét(Sh(V,K)_{F̄}, Q(Π)_λ). By the hypothesis, M ⊗ ℚ̄_ℓ ≃ (ρ^c)^{⊕d}, and ρ^c is defined over Q(Π)_λ only if the central simple algebra End_{Γ_F}(M) splits. The remark gives no argument for this. Defence: the claim is plausible (for instance, a Frobenius with an eigenvalue of multiplicity one in Q(Π)_λ would split it), and nothing depends on it.

sourceIssues.locator: Proposition 3.2.11 and its proof, published p. 146; reference [37], p. 374; arXiv v3 p. 28; v1 p. 27 (Proposition 3.2.10)
sourceIssues.printed: Proposition 3.2.11 asserts Hypothesis 3.2.10 for N ⩽ 3, and also for N > 3 provided F+ ≠ Q. Its proof assigns the case N ⩾ 3 with F+ ≠ Q to the forthcoming [37], listed as a work in preparation by Kisin, M., Shin, S.W., Zhu, Y., with a provisional title concerning cohomology of particular Shimura varieties of abelian type.
sourceIssues.correction: State the cases N ⩾ 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ of Proposition 3.2.11 as conditional on [37] (or on Hypothesis 3.2.10). Carry that condition into Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9, which all assume F⁺ ≠ ℚ, for every n ⩾ 2 and not only for n ⩾ 3, since N = n₁ ⩾ 3 always occurs; and into Corollaries 8.2.3 and 8.2.5 whenever F⁺ ≠ ℚ. As printed, those corollaries assume only '(c) F⁺ ≠ ℚ if n ⩾ 3'. Their remaining case n = 2, F⁺ = ℚ does not use [37], because Hypothesis 3.2.10 for N = 2, 3 over ℚ comes from [48] and [64], but it has its own gap, E105.
sourceIssues.reason: For N > 3 the proposition is proved only by a forward reference to a work that the bibliography lists as 'in preparation' with a temporary title. Nothing in the paper establishes it. It is used as a known input: the proof of Corollary 8.2.3 (p. 314) says 'By Proposition 3.2.11 and (c), Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known in this case'. Remark 1.1.10 (p. 113) explains that the assumption F^+ ≠ ℚ for n ≥ 3 in Theorems 1.1.5 and 1.1.9 is there because Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known for N ≥ 4 only when F^+ ≠ ℚ. Defence: the dependence is stated openly. Whether the later Kisin–Shin–Zhu work establishes exactly Hypothesis 3.2.10 in this generality was not checked here. Independent check: Checked on the image of p. 146 and in the bibliography, p. 374: '[37] Kisin, M., Shin, S.W., Zhu, Y.: Cohomology of certain Shimura varieties of abelian type (temporary title) (in preparation)'. The proof says 'The case for N ⩾ 3 when F⁺ ≠ ℚ will be proved in [37]', so N = 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ is deferred too; [64], Rogawski's Picard-surface work, covers only F⁺ = ℚ. Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 assume Hypothesis 3.2.10 for n and n+1 and are fine as conditional statements. The unconditional results take the hypothesis from Proposition 3.2.11: Corollary 8.2.3 on p. 314 ('By Proposition 3.2.11 and (c), Hypothesis 3.2.10 is known'), Corollary 8.2.5, and Theorems 1.1.1, 1.1.5, 1.1.7 and 1.1.9. All of these assume F⁺ ≠ ℚ and need N = n₁ ⩾ 3, so each depends on [37] for every n ⩾ 2, including n = 2. The KSZ paper that did appear (arXiv:2110.05381, 'The stable trace formula for Shimura varieties of abelian type') proves only a Frobenius–Hecke trace formula. Its §0.2 says: 'We intend to work out the details in a sequel', and lists LTXZZ among the intended applications. So it does not itself establish Hypothesis 3.2.10.
sourceIssues.correctionAsExtracted: State the cases N ⩾ 3 with F⁺ ≠ ℚ of Proposition 3.2.11 as conditional on [37] (or on Hypothesis 3.2.10). sourceIssues.locator: Definition 3.3.4, footnote 11, published p. 147; arXiv v3 p. 28 (footnote 11)
sourceIssues.printed: The source claims equivalence with requiring [F+q : Qp] to be odd for each prime q of F+ lying above p and inert in F.
sourceIssues.correction: Delete the footnote or replace it with a correct criterion. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭 (for ι_p inducing 𝔭), and H ⊆ Gal(M/ℚ) the subgroup generated by the stabilizers of the CM types of F. Then 𝔭 is very special inert iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to something else: that some CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ satisfies σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, which is condition (P3)/(PI3) of §§6–7.
sourceIssues.reason: (i) The footnote's condition does not imply very special. Take F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))) (minimal polynomial x⁴ + 6x² + 7, Galois group D_4, F^+ = ℚ(√2)) and p = 17. Then 17 = 𝔭𝔮 in F^+, with √2 ≡ 6 at 𝔭. At 𝔭, −3 + √2 ≡ 3 is a non-square mod 17, so 𝔭 is inert in F. At 𝔮, −3 + √2 ≡ 8 = 5², so 𝔮 splits in F. 17 is odd and unramified in F (the polynomial discriminant is 2^{10}·7), and 𝔭 has degree 1, so 𝔭 is special inert. The only prime above 17 that is inert in F is 𝔭, of odd degree 1, so the footnote declares 𝔭 very special. But the CM types of F are primitive with reflex fields of real quadratic subfield ℚ(√7) (√7 = √(−3+√2)·√(−3−√2)), so ⋂_Φ F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Hence F_rflx = F(√7) = M and F^+_rflx = ℚ(√2, √7). Since (7/17) = −1, 𝔭 is inert in F^+_rflx/F^+ and is not very special. (ii) Very special does not imply the footnote's condition. Take F a CM octic field with Gal(M/ℚ) = W(B_4) = (ℤ/2)^4 ⋊ S_4 (a generic F = F^+(√−δ) with F^+ an S_4-quartic). Then H = {(ε, π) : Σε_i even}, which has index 2 and contains c, so 𝔭 is very special iff the number of primes of F^+ above p that are inert in F is even. A Frobenius σ = ((1,1,0,0), (2 3)) (it exists by Chebotarev) gives 𝔭 inert of degree 1, 𝔮 inert of degree 2 and 𝔮′ split of degree 1. There are two inert primes, so 𝔭 is very special, but 𝔮 has even degree. Moreover σ² interchanges τ and τ^c for the embeddings above 𝔮, so no CM type is σ²-stable and (P3) fails. Defence: no proof uses the footnote. Lemma 8.1.4 uses only 'φ_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx)', which is the definition. In the cases of Remark 1.1.8 (F Galois or containing an imaginary quadratic field) the definition and the footnote both reduce to 'special inert'. The footnote does mislead anyone checking hypothesis (a) of Theorem 1.1.7. Independent check: Footnote 11 and the definitions were checked on the image of p. 147. Let M be the Galois closure of F, σ the Frobenius at 𝔭, and H = ⟨Stab Φ⟩, which is normal. Then Gal(M/F_rflx) = Gal(M/F) ∩ H, so a special inert 𝔭 is very special iff σc ∈ H. The footnote's condition is equivalent to the existence of Φ ∋ τ_∞ with σ²Φ = Φ, i.e. (P3). I checked all of this by machine: I enumerated every σ with σ(τ_∞) = τ_∞^c in D₄ and in W(B₄). There the footnote condition is always equivalent to (P3), while 'very special' differs in both directions. (i) D₄: x⁴+6x²+7 has discriminant 2¹⁰·7. Mod 17 it factors as (x−5)(x+5)(x²−3), H = V₄ ∋ c, and ⋂F_Φ = ℚ(√7). Since (7/17) = −1, the degree-one prime inert in F is not very special, though it meets the footnote. Small slip: for F = ℚ(√(−(3+√2))), the inert prime is the one with √2 ≡ −6 mod 17 (−3−√2 ≡ 3); at √2 ≡ 6, −3−√2 ≡ 8 = 5², which splits. The conclusion is unchanged after relabelling. (ii) Explicit W(B₄) instance: F⁺ = ℚ(α) with α⁴−4α²−α+1 = 0, which is totally real with disc 1957 and group S₄, and F = F⁺(√−(α+4)). Since N(α+4) = 197 is not a square in ℚ(√1957), Gal = W(B₄); Frobenius cycle-type frequencies for p < 20000 match. H is the even-sign subgroup, M^H = ℚ(√197) and F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197). At p = 43, f ≡ (x−3)(x−11)·(quadratic), and the degree-8 polynomial has type [1,1,2,4]. 𝔭 = (43, α−11) is special inert, since −(α+4) ≡ 28 is a non-square, and it splits in F⁺_rflx because 197 ≡ 5² mod 43. So 𝔭 is very special, but the degree-2 prime above 43 is inert in F: the footnote fails, and no CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ has ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. No proof cites the footnote. Versions: absent in v1/v2; present in v3 (composite definition), where example (i) still refutes it.

sourceIssues.locator: Definition 3.3.2, published p. 147 (and its use in Definition 8.1.1 (L5-2), p. 303, and in the choice of 𝔭 in the proofs of Theorem 8.2.2, p. 310, and Theorem 8.3.2, pp. 318–319); arXiv v3 p. 28
sourceIssues.printed: The source defines the reflexive closure Frflx of F by adjoining to F the intersection of all FΦ, indexed by the CM types Φ of F, and taking the resulting subfield of C.
sourceIssues.correction: Make the Chebotarev choice in §8 give (PI3). Options: (1) restore the v1–v3 composite, and correct Remarks 1.1.8 and 3.3.3 for non-Galois F. (2) Define F_rflx := F·F̃_{Φ₀}, where F̃_{Φ₀} is the Galois closure of the reflex field of one fixed CM type Φ₀. Then Frob_𝔭 fixing F⁺_rflx gives σ_𝔭 = c·h with h stabilizing Φ₀ and cΦ₀, hence σ_𝔭² does too, which is (PI3). This keeps F_rflx = F when F is Galois or contains an imaginary quadratic field K (take Φ₀ induced from K). (3) Keep the definition, add Frob_𝔭|_M = c to the Chebotarev conditions, and prove compatibility, e.g. M ∩ F⁺^{(m)}F_S ⊆ F_rflx. Options (1) and (2) narrow 'admissible' and 'very special'.
sourceIssues.reason: In the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 (p. 310), γ is taken in the image of Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) by (L5-2), and then 'by the Chebotarev density theorem' a γ-associated place is chosen whose prime 𝔭 is special inert and satisfies (PI1)–(PI7). Condition (PI3) (p. 287) requires a CM type Φ ∋ τ_∞ with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}, i.e. σ_𝔭² ∈ Stab(Φ). The same choice is made on pp. 318–319. Under the published definition, Frob_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) only gives σ_𝔭c ∈ H (the group generated by the CM-type stabilizers), and example (ii) of the footnote-11 issue gives such 𝔭 with no σ²-stable CM type. In addition, a γ-associated place is constrained only on F^{(m)}_+ and F_S, so its Frobenius on M must be imposed separately, and the paper does not address whether that is compatible. Under the v1–v3 definition, a lift of γ to Gal(F̄/F^+_rflx) = Gal(F̄/M^+) acts on M as c, so (PI3) is automatic. Defence: if F is Galois or contains an imaginary quadratic field (Remark 1.1.8), every special inert prime satisfies (PI3). For generic data M is linearly disjoint from F^{(m)}_+F_S over F, and Frob_𝔭|_M = c can be imposed. Independent check: Checked on the images of p. 147 (intersection definition), p. 303 ((L5-2) with F′ = F⁺_rflx), p. 287 ((PI3)) and pp. 310, 318–319. There γ is taken in the image of Gal(F̄/F⁺_rflx), and 'by the Chebotarev density theorem' a γ-associated special inert 𝔭 satisfying (PI1)–(PI7) is chosen; then 'remaining data in Sect. 5.1 with ℚ_p^Φ = ℚ_{p²}'. F_rflx enters the paper only through (L5-2), Lemma 8.1.4 and these choices of γ, so its only role is to deliver (PI3)/(PII3). No hypothesis of Theorems 8.2.2/8.3.2 supplies (PI3) otherwise: not the §7.1 setup, not Hypothesis 3.2.10, not (L1)–(L7). The implicit argument makes Frob_𝔭 fix F⁺_rflx, which is compatible with γ because γ comes from Gal(F̄/F⁺_rflx). Under the published intersection this only gives σ_𝔭 ∈ c·(Gal(M/F) ∩ H), which does not imply (PI3). The explicit W(B₄) field of E31 shows this: 𝔭 = (43, α−11) splits in F⁺_rflx = F⁺(√197), yet no CM type satisfies ℚ_43^Φ = ℚ_{43²}. Chebotarev gives such Frobenius classes a positive density inside the set the argument allows. Under v1–v3, F_rflx is the composite of F and all F_Φ, which equals M since only the identity fixes every CM type. There Frob_𝔭 ∈ Gal(F̄/M⁺) gives σ_𝔭 = c, so (PI3) is automatic. Imposing Frob_𝔭|_M = c directly is compatible when M ∩ F⁺^{(m)}F_S ⊆ F_rflx, e.g. for linearly disjoint (generic) data. It is not implied by (L1)–(L7) in general: if M ⊆ F⁺^{(m)}, then γ fixes Frob|_M. So a full repair may require narrowing (L5-2) and 'very special'. Versions: v1–v3 use the composite, and the change appears only in the published version, together with footnote 11.
searched: arXiv:1912.11942 v1 (December 2019), v2 and v3 (August 2021) at the same place: v1, v2 (p. 28) and v3 (p. 28) define F_rflx as 'the subfield of C generated by F and F_Φ for every CM type Φ of F'. With that definition Remark 3.3.3's 'F contains an imaginary quadratic field ⇒ F_rflx = F' is false for non-Galois F, which is presumably why the published version switched to the intersection.

sourceIssues.printed: The source says that the quasi-polarization λ induces an OS-bilinear pairing, and that its being perfect is equivalent to λ being p-principal.
sourceIssues.correction: 'which is perfect if λ is p-principal, and, when p is locally nilpotent on S, only if'. Or restrict S to schemes on which p is locally nilpotent.
sourceIssues.reason: S ranges over Sch_{/ℤ_p^τ}, which includes ℚ_p^τ-schemes. sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 3.4.12 (hypotheses) and proof of (2), published pp. 153, 155; arXiv v3 p. 32; v1 p. 31 (Lemma 3.4.13)
sourceIssues.printed: The source assumes F+ lies in Qp through τ: F+ ↪ C ≃ Q̄p, with p denoting the resulting p-adic prime. In proving (2), it writes s = dimκ(ωB∨/κ,τc∞) = dimκ VD(B)τ∞ / pD(B)τc∞.
sourceIssues.correction: Add the hypothesis that 𝔭 is inert in F, and read τ as τ̲_∞. For (2), argue directly: Lie_{B,τ_∞} = 𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/𝚅𝒟(B)_{στ_∞}, so s − r = ℓ(𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/𝒟(A)_{τ_∞}) − ℓ(𝒟(B)_{στ_∞}/𝒟(A)_{στ_∞}), and στ_∞ = τ_∞^c for 𝔭 inert. This needs no polarization.
sourceIssues.reason: As stated, 𝔭 may split in F, and then (2) fails. Take F^+ = ℚ, F imaginary quadratic with p = w_1w_2 split, ϖ = p, E an ordinary elliptic curve over 𝔽̄_p with O_F-action, A = E, B = E/E[w_1], α the quotient map and β: B → E/E[p] ≅ E, so that βα = p. With τ_∞ corresponding to w_1, α_{*,τ_∞} = 0 and α_{*,τ_∞^c} is an isomorphism, so the right side of (2) is 1 − 0 = 1. But B[w^∞] ≅ E[w^∞] for both w, so the Lie ranks agree and the left side is 0. The proof uses σ^{−1}τ_∞^c = τ_∞, i.e. 𝔭 inert. Separately, its first equality s = dim ω_{B^∨,τ_∞^c} needs dim Lie_{B,τ_∞} + dim Lie_{B,τ_∞^c} = rank H^dR_1(B)_{τ_∞^c}, which holds for unitary schemes (a compatible polarization makes B[𝔭^∞] isogenous to its dual) but is not assumed in (2). Parts (1), (3) and (4) are fine; the degree computation in (3)/(4) was checked. Defence: every application (pp. 168, 170, 197, 202, 206, 210) has 𝔭 special inert and unitary A, B, and S ∈ Sch_{/𝔽_{p²}} points to the inert case. Independent check: Lemma 3.4.12 checked on the images of pp. 153–155. The hypotheses only require F⁺_𝔭 = ℚ_p, not that 𝔭 is inert in F. Split counterexample: F⁺ = ℚ, p = w₁w₂, A = E ordinary with O_F-action, B = E/E[w₁], β∘α = [p]. On Dieudonné modules α_{*,τ_∞} ≡ 0 and α_{*,τ_∞^c} is an isomorphism, so the right side of (2) is 1. But B[w^∞] ≅ E[w^∞] for both w, so the Lie ranks agree and the left side is 0. The proof's step 'ω_{B^∨,τ_∞^c} = V𝒟(B)_{τ_∞}/p𝒟(B)_{τ_∞^c}' uses στ_∞^c = τ_∞; by Notation 3.4.10(3) this holds only for 𝔭 inert. I checked the first reading's polarization-free argument: s − r = ℓ(𝒟(B)_τ/𝒟(A)_τ) − ℓ(𝒟(B)_{στ}/𝒟(A)_{στ}), and ℓ(𝒟(B)_τ/𝒟(A)_τ) = dim ker α_{*,τ} because p𝒟(B)_τ ⊆ 𝒟(A)_τ. With στ = τ^c this gives (2). In the split case στ = τ, which gives 0, consistent with the counterexample. All six uses (pp. 168, 170, 197, 202, 206, 210) sit in §§4–5, where 𝔭 is special inert (§4.1). Versions: same in v1 (Lemma 3.4.13) and v3.

sourceIssues.printed: The source claims that projectivity of (4.1) is equivalent to projectivity after base change to Q_p^Φ. Its proof cites [62, Theorem 4.4] for the first assertion, then says only the tangent sheaf computation remains and declares the theorem proved.
sourceIssues.correction: Supply a reference or argument for 'if': e.g. properness of the integral model when the generic fibre is proper, via the valuative criterion (potentially good reduction of the abelian schemes, as in Kottwitz's or Lan's treatment of PEL moduli), or via Lan's compactifications (the boundary is flat over the base). 'Only if' is trivial.
sourceIssues.reason: The proof addresses only representability and quasi-projectivity (by [RSZ21, Theorem 4.4]) and smoothness plus the tangent sheaf (deformation theory); the projectivity criterion is not mentioned. It is standard, and may be contained in [RSZ21, Theorem 4.4] (not checked here). In v1 the proof read 'This is well-known' with a sketch covering only smoothness and quasi-projectivity (via ampleness of the canonical sheaf). Lemma 4.2.4 treats the proper and non-proper cases separately, so nothing in §4 depends on the criterion.

sourceIssues.correction: l_x := {α ∈ Hom_C(H₁^dR(A₀/C)_{τ∞}, H₁^dR(A/C)_{τ∞}) | α(H₁^dR(A₀/C)_{τ∞}) ⊆ ω_{A^∨,τ∞}} = Hom_C(H₁^dR(A₀/C)_{τ∞}, ω_{A^∨,τ∞}), a line in V_x ⊗_{F,τ∞} C (the Hodge (1,−1)-part).
sourceIssues.reason: By Remark 3.4.6 the τ-part of the Hodge filtration ω_{A^∨,τ} ⊆ H₁^dR(A)_τ has rank N − r_τ. For A₀ (rank 1, signature Φ ∋ τ∞) r_{τ∞} = 1, so ω_{A₀^∨,τ∞} = 0 and the printed condition α(0) ⊆ ω_{A^∨,τ∞} is vacuous: the printed set is all of Hom_F(H₁^dR(A₀/C), H₁^dR(A/C)), not a line. For A (signature NΦ − τ∞ + τ∞^c) ω_{A^∨,τ∞} has rank 1, so Hom(H₁^dR(A₀)_{τ∞}, ω_{A^∨,τ∞}) is a line; it is the (1,−1)-part of the weight-0 Hodge structure V_x ⊗_{τ∞} C = Hom(H^{−1,0}(A₀)_{τ∞}, H^{−1,0}(A)_{τ∞} ⊕ H^{0,−1}(A)_{τ∞}), which is the negative line for the signature (N−1,1). Reading the condition at τ∞^c instead (ω_{A₀^∨,τ∞^c} = H₁^dR(A₀)_{τ∞^c} of rank 1, ω_{A^∨,τ∞^c} of rank N−1) gives a hyperplane, so no reading of the printed formula yields a line. Defence: it is a remark 'for the readers' convenience', the intended Hodge line is standard, and nothing later uses the formula.
