sourceIssues.printed: Part (2) claims that ι restricted to B_{s⋆} is a closed immersion locally on B_{s⋆}, with the indicated canonical normal bundle isomorphism. The proof calls the map injective and identifies its cokernel with ℋom(ω_{𝒜^∨,τ∞}, im α_{*,τ∞}), deducing (2). On p. 180, Theorem 4.3.5 is invoked to claim that ι_sp is a closed immersion Zariski-locally on its source.
sourceIssues.correction: (2) The restriction of ι to B_{s⋆} is unramified (i.e. étale-locally on B_{s⋆} a closed immersion), with normal bundle ℋom(ω_{𝒜^∨,τ∞}, im α_{*,τ∞}); it is a closed immersion when it is injective on geometric points, e.g. when K^p is sufficiently small (Remark 4.3.6).
sourceIssues.reason: The proof only shows that the tangent map T_{B_{s⋆}} → ι^*T_M is injective, i.e. that ι|B_{s⋆} is unramified. Zariski-locally a closed immersion fails whenever ι|B_{s⋆} is not injective on geometric points: B_{s⋆} is proper and irreducible (Theorem 4.3.5(3)), so any Zariski open U ∋ x is dense and ι(U) ∩ V must equal ι(B_{s⋆}) ∩ V for ι|U to be a closed immersion into an open V; if x′ ≠ x has ι(x′) = ι(x) = y, then ι(B_{s⋆}) has two branches at y (or ι is generically non-injective), while U is smooth at x, so U → ι(B_{s⋆}) ∩ V is not an isomorphism. Non-injectivity does occur: for N = 3 each superspecial point of M_𝔭 lies on p + 1 components ι(B_{s⋆}) indexed by the p + 1 neighbouring vertex lattices, and these p + 1 lattices give points of S_𝔭(V, K^p)(F̄_p) over one point of T_𝔭(F̄_p), a set in bijection with Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p) (Proposition 4.4.4); if p + 1 exceeds |Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p)|, two of them coincide and the corresponding B_{s⋆} passes twice through the superspecial point. Remark 4.3.6 (closed immersion for K^p sufficiently small) is consistent with this. Defence: 'locally' can be read étale-locally, which is what the proof gives; every later use (pure codimension ⌊N/2⌋, the normal bundle, the Gysin maps ι_! in Construction 4.4.9, transversality in Theorem 4.6.2) needs only unramifiedness, and in Proposition 4.5.5 the reduction still works: an unramified morphism from a smooth scheme that is bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces is étale and universally injective, hence an isomorphism. Independent check: Quotation checked on pp. 166, 168, 180 (and Remark 4.3.6, p. 169: closed immersion only 'when K^p is sufficiently small'). The proof of (2) only shows T_{B_{s⋆}} → ι^*T_M injective, i.e. ι|B_{s⋆} unramified; p. 180 then uses (2) as 'locally for the Zariski topology on the source a closed immersion'. That reading is false as soon as ι|B_{s⋆} is not injective on geometric points. Independent proof: let x ≠ x′ in B := B_{s⋆} (over κ = F̄_p) with ι(x) = ι(x′) = y, and suppose U ∋ x is open with ι|U an immersion onto Z. B is proper and irreducible, so U is dense, Z is open in the closed set ι(B), Z = ι(B) ∩ V with V ⊆ M open, and W := B ∩ ι^{-1}(V) → Z is proper. The inverse Z ≅ U ⊆ W is a section of the separated map W → Z, so U is closed in W; it is also open and W is irreducible, hence U = W ∋ x′, contradicting injectivity of U → Z. Non-injectivity occurs: for N = 3 (Vollaard–Wedhorn picture) each superspecial point lies on p + 1 curves ι(B_{s⋆}) indexed by the p + 1 neighbouring vertex lattices, which share the prime-to-p component; if two are equivalent under U(V⋆)(F⁺) (γΛ₁ = Λ₂, γ ≠ 1 by neatness), the curve of Λ₁ passes through the superspecial point twice (at v and γ^{-1}v ≠ v). By pigeonhole this happens when p + 1 > |Sh(V⋆, (iK^p)K⋆_p)|, and for a fixed away-from-p level this cardinality does not grow with p (for odd N, K⋆_p is hyperspecial and the totally definite unitary group of rank 3 is independent of p up to isomorphism), so it happens for all large inert p. Case for the defence: read étale-locally, (2) is true (unramified ⇒ étale-locally a closed immersion, Stacks 04HJ); all later uses (codimension, normal bundle, Gysin maps, transversality) need only unramifiedness, and in Proposition 4.5.5 the reduction still works (a morphism of smooth schemes bijective on geometric points and on tangent spaces is étale and universally injective, hence an isomorphism). So the statement is wrong in the sense the paper itself uses, with no downstream damage.

sourceIssues.locator: Theorem 5.4.4(2), published p. 202 (proof pp. 203–204)
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts that ι•_κ restricted to B•_{s•} is a closed immersion locally on B•_{s•}.
sourceIssues.correction: (2) should say that the restriction of ι•_κ to B•_{s•} is unramified, i.e. étale-locally on B•_{s•} a closed immersion, with the stated normal sheaf; it is a closed immersion when it is injective on geometric points, for instance when K^{p°} is sufficiently small (Remark 5.4.5(1)). This is the correction of E39, the same statement in §4. The repair the extraction proposed does not work: if x, x′ ∈ B•_{s•} have the same image, the comparison map γ′∘φ∘γ⁻¹ is only a self-quasi-p-isogeny of A• preserving λ• and η^{p•}, an element of the p-arithmetic group of such quasi-isogenies with prime-to-p level K^{p°}. It need not be an automorphism of s•, and neatness makes that group torsion-free, not trivial, so injectivity on geometric points does not follow.
sourceIssues.reason: The proof only shows that the tangent map is injective and computes its cokernel. Unramifiedness alone gives a closed immersion only étale-locally on the target, not Zariski-locally on the source (a finite étale cover of degree 2 is unramified but not locally on the source an immersion). Remark 5.4.5(1), stated without proof, asserts a closed immersion only for sufficiently small K^{p°}. Defence: the statement is true (indeed stronger) by the rigidity argument above, and only the normal-sheaf formula is used later.
sourceIssues.correctionAsExtracted: Add the argument: ι•|B•_{s•} is unramified (injective tangent map, proved) and injective on geometric points. Two points x, x′ with the same image would give γ′γ⁻¹, an automorphism of s• preserving λ• and η^{p•}, which is trivial for neat K^{p°}. Hence it is a closed immersion (B•_{s•} is proper).

sourceIssues.locator: Lemma 5.6.2(2),(3) and proof, published p. 212 (cites Lemma A.1.4(3),(4), p. 323)
sourceIssues.printed: Part (2) claims freeness over L of H^i_𝔗(M̄°_𝔭(V°, –), L) and H^i_𝔗(M̄†_𝔭(V°, –), L) for all i ∈ ℤ. Part (3) claims triviality when N is even. The proof derives (2) from Lemma A.1.4(3), and (3) from Lemma A.1.4(4) together with Construction 5.3.6.
sourceIssues.correction: Either add 'if p + 1 is invertible in L' to (2),(3), or prove that the Fermat hypersurface S has torsion-free ℤ_ℓ-cohomology for every ℓ ≠ p. Weak Lefschetz gives degrees < N − 2 and Gysin degrees > N − 2. In the middle degree, H^{N−2}(S, ℤ_ℓ)_{tors} ≅ H^{N−1}(S, ℤ_ℓ)_{tors} ≅ H^{N+1}(ℙ^{N−1}, ℤ_ℓ)_{tors} = 0. Then deduce (2),(3) for all p-coprime L from the ℚ_ℓ case.
sourceIssues.reason: Lemma 5.6.2 puts 'p + 1 invertible in L' only in part (1), but every part of Lemma A.1.4 assumes it ('Suppose that p + 1 is invertible in L'). So for L with ℓ | p + 1 the cited lemma does not apply. Moreover A.1.4(3) is called 'an immediate consequence of (2)', yet A.1.4(2) says nothing about the middle degree N − 2, where freeness needs the torsion argument above. Defence: the statements are true (smooth hypersurfaces have torsion-free ℓ-adic cohomology), and later applications take ℓ large with ℓ ∤ p(p² − 1).

Case for the defence: the conclusion j ⩽ ⌊N/2⌋ − 1 is true in both parities by the corrected argument. Independent check: Checked on pp. 217–218. Lemma 5.7.3(3) (p. 216) gives only im(pφ•^{−1})_{τ∞^c} ∩ H^dR_1(A•_1)^⊥_{τ∞} = 0. The '+1' in 'rank H_2 ⩾ rank im(pφ•^{−1})_{τ∞^c} + 1' comes from the radical H^dR_1(A•_1)^⊥_{τ∞} = 𝒱^⊣_{s•} ⊆ H_2. It describes ℋ_{t†} as the universal object, the tautological bundle of P(𝒱_{t†}).
sourceIssues.correction: Restrict (2) to N even. For N = 2r+1 the cokernel has rank r − j; the paper's own route (restricting Theorem 5.7.7(2)) gives ζ†*_{t†}((σ*(ℋ̄_{s•2}|_{P(𝒱_{t†})})) ⊗ O(1)), where ℋ̄_{s•2}|_{P(𝒱_{t†})} is an extension of ℋ_{t†} by the trivial line bundle 𝒱_{s•}^⊣ ⊗ O, so that its top Chern class is c_{r−j−1}((σ*ℋ_{t†}) ⊗ O(1)) · c₁(O(1)).
sourceIssues.reason: Rank count from the rest of the theorem: M†_𝔭 is smooth of dimension N−2; by (1) with j = 0, B†_{s•_i} is a disjoint union of P^{⌊N/2⌋−1}; the intersection component P(𝒱_{t†}) is smooth of dimension ⌊N/2⌋−j−1 and is the scheme-theoretic fibre product. So the cokernel has rank (N−2) − 2(⌊N/2⌋−1) + (⌊N/2⌋−j−1) = N − ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1: r−j−1 for N = 2r but r−j for N = 2r+1, while σ*ℋ_{t†} ⊗ O(1) has rank dim 𝒱_{t†} − 1 = ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1. Smallest case N = 3, j = 0: B†_{s•} is a finite set of reduced points on the curve M†, so the cokernel is the 1-dimensional tangent space of M†, whereas dim 𝒱_{t†} = 1 makes ℋ_{t†} = 0. The proof ('(2) follows from Theorem 5.7.7(2) and (ℋ̄^⊣_{s•1}/ℋ̄_{s•2})|_P = (ℋ̄_{s•1}/ℋ̄_{s•2})|_P ≃ O(1)') tacitly replaces ℋ̄_{s•2}|_P by ℋ_{t†} = H₂/(im(pφ•^{−1}) + H^dR_1(A•₁)^⊥_{τ_∞}), which drops the radical 𝒱_{s•}^⊣; that radical is 0 exactly when N is even. Case for the defence: Theorem 5.7.8 is used only in the proof of Proposition 5.8.8, where N is even and the statement is correct. Independent check: Checked on pp. 223–224. From Theorem 5.7.8(1) and the proof, ℋ_{t†} is the universal hyperplane of 𝒱_{t†} (ζ† sends a point to H_2/(im(pφ•^{−1}) + H^dR_1(A•_1)^⊥_{τ∞}), of rank dim 𝒱_{t†} − 1). So (σ*ℋ_{t†}) ⊗ O(1) has rank ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1. This is consistent with the use of c_{r−j−1} in Proposition 5.8.8 (p. 230). Now count dimensions. M† has dimension N−2. By Theorem 5.5.3(2), B†_{s•_i} is a disjoint union of ℙ^{⌊N/2⌋−1}. The fibre (π†_{s•})^{−1}(t†) ≅ ℙ(𝒱_{t†}) has dimension ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1. So the cokernel has rank N − ⌊N/2⌋ − j − 1: r − j − 1 for N = 2r (fine) but r − j for N = 2r+1. For N = 3 (so j = 0) no cleanness assumption is needed. M† is a curve, B†_{s•} is a finite set of reduced points, and the cokernel is the 1-dimensional T_{M†} at the point. But dim 𝒱_{t†} = 1 gives ℋ_{t†} = 0. The proof restricts Theorem 5.7.7(2), where σ*ℋ̄_{s•2} has rank ⌈(N−2j)/2⌉ − 1, which is r − j for N odd. It then silently replaces ℋ̄_{s•2}|_ℙ by ℋ_{t†}, dropping the radical 𝒱^⊣_{s•}, which is a line exactly when N is odd (p. 200). The only use is Proposition 5.8.8, where N = 2r is even and r ⩾ 2 (pp. 229–230). So no downstream effect.

Then H¹_sing may have a nonzero image in (J/F_0J)^G and the map H¹_sing → H^{2r−1}(M̄•_N,L(r−1))^G of (6) is not even defined on all of H¹_sing. Case for the defence: §6 imposes (P3) Q_p^Φ = Q_{p²} and (P2) ℓ ∤ p(p²−1), where the step is correct. Independent check: Checked on p. 235. E_2^{−1,2r} ⊆ E_1^{−1,2r} = H^{2r−2}_𝔗(M̄†_N, L(r−1)), on which Galois acts trivially by Lemma 5.6.2(3). So Frob_{F_p^Φ} acts on E_2^{−1,2r}(−1) by multiplication by q^{±1}, where q = #F_p^Φ, and the invariants are the (q−1)-torsion. In §5, F_p^Φ is only required to contain F_{p²} (§4.1: 'F_p^Φ contains F_{p²}'). The condition Q_p^Φ = Q_{p²} is imposed only by (P3) in §6 (p. 264). sourceIssues.printed: The source calls the induced map σ : Q^{†,†} → P^{†,†} a trivial P¹-bundle. In (5), f ∈ H²_T(Q̄^{†,†}, O_λ(1)) denotes the cycle class obtained from any T-orbit of sections of σ̄ : Q̄^{†,†} → P̄^{†,†}, again described as a trivial P¹-fibration.

Equivalently, Q^{†,†} = P(N_{P^{†,†}/P^{°,°}}) is the exceptional divisor of Q^{°,°} = Bl_{P^{†,†}}P^{°,°}. It has the two disjoint sections Q^{•,°} ∩ Q^{†,†} and Q^{°,•} ∩ Q^{†,†}, and it is not trivial over any connected component. In (5), 'trivial' should be deleted and f taken to be the class of one of these two sections (or of any section).
sourceIssues.reason: Near P^{†,†}, 𝐏 is x0y0 = x1y1 (= p) with M°_{nα} = {xα = 0}, and the ideal of P^{°,°} is pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) + pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1}). So 𝐐 embeds in P(pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) ⊕ pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1})). A chart computation (x0 = u·x1, y1 = u·y0, p = u·x1·y0) shows σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = {x1 = y0 = 0} is reduced, smooth and meets each fibre in a whole P¹, hence σ^{-1}(P^{†,†}) = P(pr_0^*N_0 ⊕ pr_1^*N_1). Since O(M°+M•) = O(div p) ≅ O, O(−M°)|_{M†} ≅ O_{M°}(M†)|_{M†} = N_{M†/M°}, which by Theorem 5.3.4 and Corollary 5.3.5 is O(p+1) restricted to the degree-(p+1) Fermat hypersurface DL(V_{s°}) ⊂ P(V_{s°}). Over a connected proper base, P(A ⊕ B) ≅ base × P¹ iff A ⊕ B ≅ M ⊕ M for a line bundle M (P(E) ≅ P(E′) iff E′ ≅ E ⊗ M), hence, by Atiyah's Krull–Schmidt theorem, iff A ≅ B. Here that would require pr_0^*N_0 ≅ pr_1^*N_1, and restricting to {z} × DL(V_{s°}) for a point z of M†_{n0} would make O(p+1) trivial on a Fermat hypersurface of dimension n1 − 2 ⩾ 1, where it is ample. For example, when n = 2, over a point × Fermat curve C ⊂ P² the bundle is the ruled surface P(O ⊕ O(p+1)|_C), whose sections have self-intersection ±(p+1)², so it is not C × P¹. This matches the analysis of the earlier open question U1. What fails is anything that uses a global trivialisation: e.g. independence of f from the choice of section (the two section classes differ by ±σ^*c1(pr_0^*N_0 ⊗ pr_1^*N_1^{-1})) or f² = 0. No such use was found. Independent check: Checked on p. 252 (third bullet of Lemma 5.11.3(2); (5) 'the trivial ℙ^1-fibration'). Locally, 𝐏 is x0y0 = x1y1 (= p) with M°_{nα} = {xα = 0}. In the chart x0 = u·x1 the blow-up along (x0, x1) gives y1 = u·y0 and p = u·x1·y0, so σ^{−1}(P^{†,†}) = {x1 = y0 = 0} is reduced with fibres ℙ^1. Also I ⊗ O_{P^{†,†}} is free on x0, x1, because the relation y0x0 − y1x1 dies modulo the maximal ideal. Hence Q^{†,†} = ℙ(pr_0^*O(−M°_{n0}) ⊕ pr_1^*O(−M°_{n1}))|_{P^{†,†}}. Since O(M° + M•) = O(div p) ≅ O, O(−M°)|_{M†} ≅ O_{M°}(M†)|_{M†} = N_{M†/M°}. By Corollary 5.3.5 (p. 198) this is (m^{†°})^*O_{M°}(p+1), i.e. O(p+1) on each Fermat fibre, a degree-(p+1) hypersurface in ℙ^{n−1} (Lemma A.1.4(1)). A ℙ^1-bundle ℙ(A ⊕ B) over a connected proper base is trivial iff A ≅ B. Restrict to {z} × C, with C a component of a fibre of M†_{n1} (dimension n1 − 2 ⩾ 1 since n1 = 2r1+1 ⩾ 3). There pr_0^*N_0 is trivial while pr_1^*N_1 = O(p+1)|_C is ample. For n1 = 3 this gives the ruled surface ℙ(O ⊕ O(p+1)|_C) over a Fermat curve, which has a section of self-intersection −(p+1)^2 and so is not C × ℙ^1. The bundle is therefore not trivial over any connected component. Uses: Lemma 5.11.3(3)–(5) feed Lemma 7.2.5(2),(4),(6) (pp. 289–291) and Theorem 7.2.8(1a)–(1d) (pp. 293–295). These need only a ℙ^1-bundle with a Galois-stable section, for Leray–Hirsch and Galois-equivariance of the splitting. The two canonical sections Q^{•,°} ∩ Q^{†,†} and Q^{°,•} ∩ Q^{†,†} (fourth bullet) serve. The class f enters only through the decomposition in (5), which holds for any section class. No argument uses f² = 0 or independence of f from the section. So nothing downstream is affected. sourceIssues.reason: Both steps are standard, and the conclusion is correct; they are asserted without argument.

With r(t)v = v + xv′ one gets x(s′ − p²s) = 0 ⇔ x(s − p^{−2r})(s + p^{−2r}) = 0 ⇔ x(s − p^{−2r}) = 0 (ℓ odd), as stated. This agrees with [51, proof of Proposition 3.5.2] (arXiv:2108.06998v1, p. 28): in the basis where r^♮(φ_q²) = diag(q^{−N}(1+x)(1+y)⁻¹, q^{−N+2}(1+y)(1+x)⁻¹), r^♮(t) = 1 + (0 0; x_0 0), so t sends the q^{−N}-eigenvector e_1 to e_1 + x_0e_2. sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.3.4(3), published p. 285
sourceIssues.printed: The source deduces (3) from (1) and (P4), which it reads as making P_{α(Π_𝔭)} mod λ^m special for level raising at 𝔭. It asserts the O_λ[Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})]-module isomorphism H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, O_λ(r)) ≃ H ⊗_{R^ram} R_1(r).
sourceIssues.correction: Read the left side as localised at 𝔪, and let R_1 ⊆ (R^ram)^{⊕N} be the r^♮_ram(φ_p²)-stable complement of R^ram v ⊕ R^ram v′; inertia acts trivially on it. Then H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, O_λ(r))_𝔪 = E_2^{0,2r−1} = Gr_0 H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄_N, RΨO_λ(r))_𝔪 ≅ H ⊗_{R^ram} R_1(r). Proof: (a) F_{−1} and H/F_0 (E_2^{1,2r−2} and E_2^{−1,2r}) have Frobenius eigenvalues p² and 1 by Lemma 5.6.2. By (P4) these are separated modulo λ from the eigenvalues on R_1(r), so H ⊗ R_1(r) ⊆ Gr_0. (b) The {1,p²}-block has zero image in Gr_0: rationally because the monodromy x is nonzero at every characteristic-zero point of R^ram, and integrally because Gr_0 is O_λ-free by part (2).
sourceIssues.reason: The symbol R_1 appears nowhere else in the paper, and the displayed isomorphism — which is the entire content of the proof of (3) — is asserted without argument. In the text layer of pub/v1/v2/v3, R_1 occurs only in this line, so it is never defined. The left side also lacks the localisation at 𝔪 that part (3) concerns. The displayed isomorphism is all the proof of (3) has, and it is not immediate. By Lemma 5.9.3(1), E_1^{0,2r−1} = H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N, L(r)) and the odd-degree terms of M°, M† vanish, so H^{2r−1}_𝔗(M̄•_N)_𝔪 = E_2^{0,2r−1} = Gr_0 of H^{2r−1}_𝔪 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram)^{⊕N}(r) (p. 282). sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Theorem 6.3.4(5), published pp. 285–286
sourceIssues.printed: The source claims O_λ/λ^m = R^ram/𝔫. Its justification is that 𝔫 ∩ O_λ = λ^m O_λ, so the structure map O_λ → R^ram yields the equality O_λ/λ^m = R^ram/𝔫.
sourceIssues.correction: Add to Theorem 6.3.4(5) the hypothesis that P_{α(Π_v)} mod λ^m is level-raising special at v (Definition 3.1.5) for every v ∈ Σ⁺_lr. Equivalently, ρ̄^{(m)}_{Π,λ,+} satisfies 𝒟^ram at Σ⁺_lr; this holds vacuously if Σ⁺_lr = ∅. In the proof, read 𝔫 O_λ-linearly, as the kernel of O_λ ⊗ T^{Σ⁺∪Σ⁺_p}_N → O_λ/λ^m. With these, ρ_{Π,λ,+} mod λ^m is of type 𝒮^ram, and so R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^m. The added hypothesis holds in both applications: Theorem 8.2.2 (Σ⁺_lr = ∅) and Theorem 8.3.2 (Σ⁺_lr = {𝔭_1}, by (PII4)).
sourceIssues.reason: As defined in Notation 6.1.3, 𝔫 is an ideal of the ℤ[‖v‖^{±1/2}]-algebra T^{Σ⁺∪Σ⁺_p}_N; read literally, λ^m need not lie in 𝔫R^ram when E_λ is ramified over the field generated by the Hecke eigenvalues. Read O_λ-linearly, R^ram/𝔫 is a quotient O_λ/λ^j of O_λ/λ^m, and j = m requires an O_λ-algebra map R^ram → O_λ/λ^m compatible with φ_Π, i.e. (Chebotarev and Carayol) that ρ_{Π,λ} mod λ^m be a lifting of type 𝒮^ram. At 𝔭 this is (P4) (mod λ^m); but at v ∈ Σ⁺_lr the local condition is 𝒟^ram, which demands P_0(T) = (T − ‖v‖^{−N})(T − ‖v‖^{−N+2}) exactly ([51, Definition 3.5.1]), whereas the hypotheses of Theorem 6.3.4 (rigidity (b), §6.1) only give this modulo λ. If Π_v is level-raising special only modulo λ^j with j < m, then R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^{j′} with j′ ⩽ j, H^{2r−1}/𝔫 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram/𝔫)^{⊕N}(r) is killed by λ^{j′} (and nonzero since d_ram > 0), and the conclusion (R̄^{(m)c})^{⊕μ} with μ ⩾ 1 fails. Defence: in the applications (§8, pp. 318–319) Σ⁺_lr is either ∅ or {𝔭_1} with 𝔭_1 a previously chosen prime satisfying (PII4), i.e. level-raising special modulo λ^m, so the main theorems are unaffected; Theorem 6.3.4(4) is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked on pp. 285–286. The problem is real, but the asserted step is false in general rather than merely unjustified, and so is Theorem 6.3.4(5) as stated. So the kind should be 'error'. The argument: 𝔫 is read O_λ-linearly, which is clearly the intended reading. R^ram/𝔫 = T^ram_𝔪/𝔫 is then a quotient O_λ/λ^j of O_λ/λ^m. j = m iff φ_Π mod λ^m factors through T^ram_𝔪 ≅ R^ram. By Chebotarev and Carayol (Assumption 6.1.6), that happens iff ρ_{Π,λ,+} mod λ^m is a lifting of type 𝒮^ram. At v ∈ Σ⁺_lr the local condition is 𝒟^ram, i.e. s = ‖v‖^{−N} exactly: the paper itself writes R^ram = R^mix/(s − p^{−2r}) on p. 281. But Π_v is unramified, since Σ⁺_lr is strongly disjoint from Σ⁺_min ⊇ Σ⁺_Π. The hypotheses of Theorem 6.3.4 constrain Π_v only through rigidity (Definition 6.3.3(2): generalized eigenvalues of r̄♮_v(φ_w) in F̄_ℓ, i.e. modulo λ) and through ℓ ∤ ‖v‖(‖v‖²−1) (p. 264). (P4) is mod λ^m but only at 𝔭, and (P6)/(d) are congruences with no local content at v. So if P_{α(Π_v)} is level-raising special modulo λ^j but not λ^{j+1} with j < m, then R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^{j′} with j′ ⩽ j. In that case H^{2r−1}_ét(Sh(V′_N,…)_F̄, O_λ(r))/𝔫 ≅ H ⊗ (R^ram/𝔫)^{⊕N}(r) is nonzero (d_ram > 0) and killed by λ^{j′}. It therefore cannot be isomorphic to (R̄^{(m)c})^{⊕μ} with μ ⩾ 1, and (5) is false. The literal (ℤ-linear) reading of 𝔫 fails too, independently, when E_λ is ramified over the field of Hecke eigenvalues; that part is only a notational slip. Reach: §7 never invokes (5). §7.2 uses 6.3.4(1)–(3) (Lemma 7.2.5, pp. 289–291) and 6.3.4(4) (Theorem 7.2.8(2), p. 295). §8 invokes (5) explicitly only in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2 ((8.6), p. 312), where Σ⁺_lr,I = ∅ (p. 310). It invokes (5) implicitly in the proof of Theorem 8.3.2 ('exactly same argument for the parallel claim in the proof of Theorem 8.2.2', p. 319), where Σ⁺_lr,I = {𝔭_1}. There 𝔭_1 satisfies (PII4), 'P_{α(Π_{0,𝔭})} mod λ^m is level-raising special' (p. 298), with the same m, which is exactly the missing hypothesis. So the main theorems are unaffected. Part (4) does not use R^ram/𝔫 = O_λ/λ^m. Versions: the wording '𝔫 ∩ O_λ = λ^m O_λ' is in v1/v2 p. 120 and v3 p. 119.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition 7.2.7 and footnote 29, published p. 292
sourceIssues.printed: The source invokes [47, Theorem 2.16 and Theorem 2.18] to reduce the proof to the coefficient ring O_λ having the property called very nice in [47, Definition 2.15] for 𝔼^{p,q}_{s,(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)}. Footnote 29 says that [47] assumes properness over the base for the strictly semistable X, but Lemma 7.2.5(6) allows those proofs to apply unchanged to the nonproper 𝐐.
sourceIssues.correction: State and prove [47, Theorems 2.16, 2.18] for Λ = O_λ and for strictly semistable 𝐐 that need not be proper, with nearby-cycle cohomology H_𝔗(Q̄, RΨ) in place of generic-fibre cohomology. The inputs are Lemmas 5.11.2, 5.11.3 and 7.2.5(6). Define cl(Q_sp) as the image of the cycle class of Q_sp (the flat closure of 𝐐^η_sp) in C^n(Q, O_λ), i.e. [47]'s e_z. Justify its restriction to Q^{(0)} as the geometric class of Q_sp ×_𝐐 Q̄^{(0)}, as used in Theorem 7.2.8(3), via [47, Proposition 2.19] or a pushforward argument along 𝐌_𝔭(V°_n, K°_sp) → 𝐏. Correct footnote 22: C^r(Q, L) is the coinvariant version of [47]'s A^r(Q, L)^0; the two agree under (N3).
sourceIssues.reason: Point (a): the inputs a proof would need are available — Lemma 5.11.2 (specialization isomorphisms via Lan–Stroh [43, Cor. 5.20]), Lemma 7.2.5(6) (compactly supported = ordinary cohomology on the localized strata, which restores Poincaré duality), and finiteness over O_λ. Continuous O_λ-cohomology is the limit of the ℤ/ℓ^ν-cases, as in the proof of [47, Lemma 2.6]. Point (b): Q_sp has dimension n and its singular locus lies over the †-stratum of 𝐌_𝔭(V°_n, K°_sp), which has dimension ⩽ n−2, so the codimension condition (⩾ n+1 in the (2n−1)-dimensional components of Q_κ) is plausible, but the finite map 𝐌_𝔭(V°_n,K°_sp) → 𝐏 need not be an embedding, and the paper says nothing about it. Point (c): under (N3), which the proof itself verifies, invariants → coinvariants is an isomorphism on B^n(Q,O_λ)^0_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)} ⊆ H^{2n}(Q̄^{(0)}), so (c) is harmless. In the defence: none of this is likely to fail. But a black-box theorem is being used outside its stated hypotheses with only a one-line justification, and a formalisation must either reprove [47, Theorems 2.16, 2.18] for this setting or supply the extension. Independent check: Quote and footnote 29 checked on p. 292. From arXiv:1511.08268v2: §2 opens 'Throughout this section, the coefficient ring Λ will be either Q_p or Z/p^ν for some ν ≥ 1' (p. 5). §2.2 and §2.4 assume 'X a proper strictly semistable scheme' (pp. 7, 12). Definition 2.15 ((N1)–(N3)), Theorem 2.16, Theorem 2.18 (η^r_𝔪(e_z) = ∂(α_𝔪(z)), with e_z the class of the flat closure z♯) and Proposition 2.19 match the numbering LTXZZ cite. LTXZZ apply them with Λ = O_λ and a possibly non-proper 𝐐. Footnote 29 addresses only properness, and only by assertion. Point (a) is confirmed. In LTXZZ's favour: Lemma 5.11.3 gives strict semistability, Lemma 5.11.2 (via Lan–Stroh) replaces proper base change, Lemma 7.2.5(6) supplies H_c = H after localisation, and O_λ is a limit of O_λ/λ^k. Point (b) needs one correction: cl(Q_sp) is introduced, on p. 291 ('The cycle Q_sp gives rise to a class cl(Q_sp) ∈ C^n(Q, L)'), but its construction is not specified. For [47, Theorem 2.18] to give Proposition 7.2.7 it must be e_z. The proof of Theorem 7.2.8(3) (p. 295) then evaluates it as a geometric class: '∇(cl(Q_sp)) = ∇(cl(Q•_△)) with cl(Q•_△) ∈ H^{2n}_𝔗(Q^{•,•}, O_λ(n))'. That identification is what [47, Proposition 2.19] provides under a codimension condition on the singular locus of Z_i, and neither the proposition nor its hypothesis is mentioned. Point (c) is confirmed: [47] v2 p. 7 has A^j(X_κ,Λ)^? = (B^j(X_κ,Λ)^?)^{G_κ} (invariants), whereas p. 262 here has C^r(Q, L) := B^r(Q, L)^0_{Gal} (coinvariants). Footnote 22 (p. 263) nevertheless equates C^r with A^r(Q, L)^0. This is harmless under (N3), which the proof verifies. None of (a)–(c) is likely to fail, but a black-box theorem is used outside its stated hypotheses with a one-line justification, so 'gap / the proof' is right. Versions: v1/v2 footnote 20 cites 'Lemma 7.2.4(6)'; v3 footnote 29 cites 'Lemma 7.2.5(6)'.

sourceIssues.correction: It is an isomorphism only after localization at (𝔪₀,𝔪₁), and this needs an argument. That suffices, since the statement is modulo (𝔫₀,𝔫₁). For the smooth proper model X = 𝐌_{n₀} ×_{𝐓_𝔭} 𝐌_{n₁} over ℤ_{p²}, the localization sequence and absolute purity give 0 → H^{2n}(X_s, O_λ(n)) → H^{2n}(X_{ℚ_{p²}}, O_λ(n)) → H^{2n−1}(X_s, O_λ(n−1)) → 0. After localization H^{2n−1}(X_s, O_λ(n−1))_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)} = (V(−1))^{Gal(F̄_p/F_{p²})}, with V := H^{2n−1}(X̄_s, O_λ(n))_{(𝔪₀,𝔪₁)} (the H¹-term vanishes because the localized H^{2n−2} is 0 by Assumption 7.3.2). This is 0, since V is O_λ-free and V(−1) ⊗ E_λ is pure of weight 1.
sourceIssues.reason: In the proof's own Hochschild–Serre sequence, H^{2n}_𝔗(M_{n₀}×_{T_𝔭}M_{n₁}, O_λ(n)) is absolute cohomology of the special fibre over F_{p²} (Notation 3.3.6(5)). Without localization it differs from the degree-2n absolute cohomology of the generic fibre over F_𝔭 = ℚ_{p²} by the quotient H^{2n−1}(X_s, O_λ(n−1)). That quotient is nonzero in general: it contains H¹(F_{p²}, H^{2n−2}(X̄_s, O_λ(n−1))), which picks up the Tate classes (for instance powers of an ample class) — so the unlocalized assertion is false. The natural comparison map also runs the other way (restriction from the integral model to the generic fibre). The direction printed is that of loc′_𝔭 in Construction 4.6.1, whose middle arrow H^i(𝐌^η) → H^i_𝔗(M, RΨL) is not spelled out there. In the defence: everything in Theorem 7.3.4 is modulo (𝔫₀,𝔫₁), hence localized at (𝔪₀,𝔪₁), and the localized comparison holds by the weight argument above (the same weight input underlies (7.3)). If H_𝔗(M, ·) is read as Gal(ℚ̄_p/ℚ_{p²})-hypercohomology, the map is an isomorphism by construction, but then the Hochschild–Serre sequence with H¹(F_{p²}, ·) in the same proof needs the localized comparison instead. Either way the theorem stands.

sourceIssues.printed: The source uses (L5-2) together with Lemma 2.7.1 to select (γ1, γ2, ξ), producing γ. It then invokes Sect. 2.6 and Proposition 2.6.6, taking m0 = mΣ and rS = 1, to select Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ} that is (S, γ)-abundant.
sourceIssues.correction: Choose γ after S and adapted to it. If F_S is Galois over F⁺ with c·s = εs, require that the eigenvalue b(γ) of a lift of γ on (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} equals ε. In the elliptic case (Corollary 8.2.3) this is arranged by replacing γ with γ·ρ̄₊(z), where (ρ̄_{A₀}, ρ̄_{A₁}, ε̄)(z) = (−1, 1, 1); this preserves Lemma 2.7.1(a)–(e). In rank 0, take S inside one c-eigenspace. In rank 1, use γ at 𝔭₁ (with b matching the component of the Abel–Jacobi class with unit coefficient) and γz at 𝔭₂ when the second basis vector lies in the other eigenspace, instead of one abundant pair for a single γ. Base-change situations whose image has no central −1 need a further argument.
sourceIssues.reason: This is how E1 (Lemma 2.6.4) enters §8. Let γ̃ run over lifts of γ to Gal(F̃_S/F⁺) and let 2g be the order of γ on F^{(m)}. For a γ-associated place, Ψ_{w^{(m)}} = γ̃^{2g}|_{F_S}, which commutes with γ̃; so G_{S,γ} is contained in the restriction of the σ-fixed part of Gal(F̃_S/F_+^{(m)}), σ = conjugation by γ̃. Suppose ρ̄ extends to r̄: Γ_{F⁺} → GL(R̄) (the base-change situation, e.g. Corollary 8.2.3, where R = Sym^{n0−1} ⊗ Sym^{n1−1}(n) comes from F⁺), and S = O_λ·s with c·s = εs. Then F_S is Galois over F⁺, θ_S(σ(τ))(s) = ε r̄(γ̃) θ_S(τ)(s), and r̄(γ̃) acts on the line (R̄^{(m)})^{h_γ} by some b = ±1 determined by γ. If εb = −1, then θ_S(Ψ)(s) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}: no (S,γ)-abundant element exists, loc_w(s1) = 0 at every γ-associated place, and the 𝔭-bullet of the pairing computation fails. This is the mechanism of E1's example (R = ℤ_3(1), S from a unit of F⁺, γ = complex conjugation). Nothing in Lemma 2.7.1(a)–(e), which is all the proof requires of γ, relates b to the c-sign of S, and γ is chosen without regard to S. Defence: when ρ̄ ≇ ρ̄^c, F_S and F_{S^c} are essentially independent over F_+^{(m)} and G_{S,γ} is as large as Lemma 2.6.4 claims (up to a bounded defect); in the elliptic case of Corollary 8.2.3 (both ranks) the sign can be corrected by the central element as indicated, and in rank 0 a suitable generator of S can be chosen instead. In a base-change situation without a central −1 in the image (e.g. Π_α base changes in Corollary 8.2.5, where (L5-1) comes from Lemma 2.3.5(b)), the rank-one argument, in which s is fixed by the cycle, needs a further idea. The printed proofs address none of this. Independent check: Checked on pp. 133–137, 310, 317–319. The mechanism is correct and hits the printed proofs. Let σ ∈ Γ_{F⁺} be a Frobenius above a γ-associated place, so Ψ = σ^{2g}|_{F_S} (g the order of h_γ). Suppose s ∈ H^1(F, R̄) satisfies c·s = εs for an extension r̄ of ρ̄ to Γ_{F⁺}; r̄ factors through Gal(F₊^{(m)}/F⁺) since ker ρ̄₊ ⊆ ker ρ̄. The cocycle relation on ker r̄ gives s(σ^{2g}) = εr̄(σ)s(σ^{2g}), and by (c) R̄^{r̄(σ)²} is a free rank-one line on which r̄(σ) acts by b = b(γ) = ±1. If εb = −1 then θ_S(Ψ)(s) = 0 for every Ψ ∈ G_{S,γ}; since H^1_ns(F_w, R̄) → R̄ (evaluation at Ψ) is injective, loc_w(s) = 0 at every γ-associated w, and no abundant element exists. In the elliptic setting of Corollary 8.2.3, both signs are admissible. On R̄₁ = Sym^{2r₁}H^1(A₁)(r₁) the fixed line is the middle weight and b₁ = +1. On R̄₀ = Sym^{2r₀−1}H^1(A₀)(r₀), replacing σ by σz with (ρ̄_{A₀}, ρ̄_{A₁}, ε̄)(z) = (−1, 1, 1) (such z exists in Γ_{FF′} for large ℓ) negates r̄(σ), since n₀ − 1 is odd. The element z is central in im ρ̄₊ with z² = 1, so h_γ, ξ, the prime-to-ℓ orders and (a)–(e) of Lemma 2.7.1 are unchanged, while b flips. Since the proofs pick γ from (a)–(e) alone, after S, one of the two admissible choices fails for S in an eigenspace. In rank 0 the hypothetical S may lie in either eigenspace. In rank 1 the Abel–Jacobi class s lies in the eigenspace of the vanishing L-factor when the other Selmer part vanishes. So the reliance on Proposition 2.6.6 is a genuine hole. Repairs. Rank 0: take S c-stable inside one eigenspace and replace γ by γz if needed. Rank 1: a single γ does not suffice when S meets both eigenspaces (then s₂ is invisible at every γ-associated place), but the argument permits different elements at the two primes: take 𝔭₁ γ-associated with b(γ) matching the component of s with unit coefficient, and 𝔭₂ γz-associated. Then loc_{𝔭₁}(s₂) = 0 automatically, loc_{𝔭₂}(s₂) is large, and (PI)/(PII) depend only on h_γ and ξ. The first reading's alternative (a generator with both components) works only if both eigenspaces of the Selmer group are nonzero. When R̄ ≇ R̄^c as Γ_F-modules, F_S and its conjugate are disjoint up to bounded defect (Goursat), and Lemma 2.6.4 holds up to that defect, so the problem is confined to essentially self-dual (e.g. base-change) R. In base-change cases without a central −1 in the image (the setting of Corollary 8.2.5, where (L5-1) comes from Lemma 2.3.5(b)), no repair is available from the paper.

Theorem 8.2.2 applies only to admissible λ. So for n = 2 and F⁺ = ℚ, which (c) allows, the proofs establish nothing. In arXiv v1/v2 this case was covered: Definition 8.1.1 defined 'weakly admissible' ((L1)–(L5)), Theorem 8.2.1 treated weakly admissible λ when n = 2, and the elliptic-curve proposition (v1 Proposition 8.1.5) gave weak admissibility for almost all ℓ without F⁺ ≠ ℚ. v3 deleted weak admissibility but left '(c) F⁺ ≠ ℚ if n ⩾ 3'. Corollary 8.2.3 assumes '(c) F⁺ ≠ Q if n ⩾ 3' and is proved by 'Theorem 8.2.2 and Lemma 8.1.3 (where we use (a) and (c))'. But Lemma 8.1.3 assumes 'F⁺ ≠ Q' unconditionally, and Lemma 8.1.4 (used for Corollary 8.2.5) has hypothesis '(c) F⁺ ≠ Q'. Both need it for (L7) through Corollary D.1.4 ('Suppose that F⁺ ≠ Q'). Theorem 8.2.2 applies only to admissible λ, which includes (L7). So for n = 2 and F⁺ = Q, which both corollaries allow, the published text proves nothing. The clause '(c) … if n ⩾ 3' only covers Hypothesis 3.2.10 (Proposition 3.2.11 gives N ⩽ 3 for any F⁺). Version check: v1 has 'weakly admissible' ((L1–L5)), Theorem 8.2.1 treats 'n = 2 and λ weakly admissible', and its intro theorems carry '[F⁺ : Q] > 1 if n ≥ 3'. v3 (= published) deleted weak admissibility and changed Theorems 1.1.1/1.1.7 to 'F⁺ ≠ Q', but kept '(c) F⁺ ≠ Q if n ⩾ 3' in Corollaries 8.2.3/8.2.5. Remark 1.1.10 only asserts that a 'slightly different argument' exists for n = 2. The statements are plausibly true, but that case is not proved in the published paper.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Theorem 8.2.2, justification of (8.5), published p. 313; the same for (8.14) in the proof of Theorem 8.3.2, p. 319
sourceIssues.printed: The source obtains (8.5) from smooth models of Sh′_n and Sh′_{n+1} over O_{F_w}, asserting that these models satisfy an analogue of Lemma 4.2.4.
sourceIssues.correction: For w above ℓ, add the argument that the Abel–Jacobi class of a cycle on a smooth proper O_{F_w}-scheme (F_w/ℚ_ℓ unramified, dimension 2n−1 with 2n ⩽ ℓ−2) lies in the Fontaine–Laffaille subgroup H¹_ns(F_w, −) of Definition 2.2.5 with torsion coefficients, e.g. via Faltings/Fontaine–Messing comparison for H^*(X ∖ Z) with X, Z smooth proper over O_{F_w}, and that Υ_i preserves H¹_ns.
sourceIssues.reason: (8.5) is claimed at every nonarchimedean w not above Σ⁺ ∪ {𝔭}, including the ℓ-adic places, and the ℓ-adic bullet of the pairing computation uses it there. Lemma 4.2.4 is a statement for p-coprime coefficient rings (specialization isomorphisms), which gives unramifiedness at w ∤ ℓ but says nothing about crystallinity of torsion classes at w | ℓ. Lemma 2.2.6 identifies H¹_ns with the preimage of the crystalline classes only for free modules, whereas c1 is a torsion class not known to lift. Defence: the needed statement is standard integral p-adic Hodge theory in the Fontaine–Laffaille range guaranteed by (L1), and when F⁺ ≠ ℚ the Shimura varieties are proper. Independent check: Checked on pp. 311–313 and 319. (8.5) is claimed for all w not above Σ⁺ ∪ {𝔭} with Σ⁺_I = Σ⁺_min (so it includes the ℓ-adic places, by (L2)), and the ℓ-adic bullet on p. 311 invokes (8.5) there. The only justification is that Sh′_n and Sh′_{n+1} have smooth models 'for which (an analogue of) Lemma 4.2.4 holds'. Lemma 4.2.4 is a specialization isomorphism for p-coprime coefficients and gives only unramifiedness at w ∤ ℓ. At w | ℓ one needs the torsion class loc_w(c₁) to lie in H^1_ns(F_w, R̄^{(m)c}) in the sense of Definitions 2.2.4–2.2.5, i.e. its extension must be a quotient of lattices in a crystalline representation. Lemma 2.2.6 does not give this, since c₁ is a torsion class obtained through Υ_i and the quotient by (𝔫₀, 𝔫₁). The fact is standard but not in the paper. Faltings' comparison for the good-reduction pair (X, Z) over O_{F_w} (F_w/Q_ℓ unramified, degree 2n − 1 ⩽ ℓ − 2 by (L1)) makes the torsion Abel–Jacobi extension torsion-crystalline. Torsion-crystalline modules in the sense of Definition 2.2.4 are closed under subquotients and direct sums, so the pushout along Υ_i stays crystalline. Same sentence in v1 ('Lemma 4.1.4') and v3.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition A.2.4(2), published p. 328
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts that π^{−1}(S) is a singleton for any morphism S → DL(V♯) \ DL(V♯)′, whereas a special point s has π^{−1}(s) = P(H_s^⊨) ≃ P^{r−1}_κ. It concludes that π blows up DL(V♯)′ and names E ⊆ D̃L(V) as its exceptional divisor.
sourceIssues.correction: Describe D̃L(𝒱) as the closed subscheme of the ℙ^{r−1}-bundle of hyperplanes H_2 ⊂ H^⊨ over DL(𝒱♯) cut out by H_2 ⊆ 𝒱, i.e. by the vanishing on H_2 of the projection ℓ: H^⊨ → O·1. This needs H^⊨ handled as a subbundle, e.g. through the F_{p²}-structure. Then show that ℓ, as a section of (H^⊨)^∨ (rank r) on the smooth r-dimensional DL(𝒱♯), has as zero scheme exactly the reduced set DL(𝒱♯)′: a transversality check at the (p+1)(p³+1)⋯(p^{2r−1}+1) special points. The standard description of the blow-up along the zero scheme of a regular section then identifies π with Bl_{DL(𝒱♯)′}, gives E as the exceptional divisor and gives O_E(E) ≅ O_E(−1).
sourceIssues.reason: A proper morphism that is an isomorphism away from finitely many smooth points and has fibres P^{r−1} over them need not be the blow-up (D̃L(V) could a priori be non-reduced or non-normal along E); the blow-up structure is used for ℒ|_E ≃ O_E(−E) = O_E(1) and for c_1(O(E))|_E = −η in (A.3)–(A.4), which determine the value of the integral. Case for the defence: the deformation argument of Proposition A.1.3(2) presumably adapts to show D̃L(V) smooth, all other steps of (A.1)–(A.5) check out, the case r = 1 is confirmed directly (−p = d•_{1,p}), and the numbers d•_{r,q} are exactly those making Proposition B.3.5(3) factor, so the stated result is very likely correct. Independent check: Quotation checked on p. 328. The inference 'In particular, π is a blow-up along DL(𝒱♯)′' is drawn only from the fibre data: π is an isomorphism off the special points, with fibre ℙ^{r−1} over each. That data does not determine a blow-up. Counterexample: take X a smooth surface and Z the curvilinear length-2 point (x, y²). Then Bl_Z X = {xt = y²s} is an isomorphism off the point with reduced fibre ℙ^1 over it, but it is singular and its exceptional Cartier divisor is 2·ℙ^1. Intersection numbers like those in (A.3)–(A.5), which use O_E(E) ≅ O_E(−1) and c_1(O(E))|_E = −η, would change. The paper gives no scheme-theoretic analysis of D̃L(𝒱). Note also that H^⊨ is a left orthogonal for a pairing σ-linear in the first variable, and in families over non-perfect bases this need not be a subbundle, so the functor as written needs care. A correct route is in the correction. Case for the defence: the result is very likely true. The first reading reports that r = 1 checks directly (−p = d•_{1,p}) and that the numbers d•_{r,q} are the ones that make Proposition B.3.5(3) factor. I did not independently recheck these. The remaining steps (A.1)–(A.5) follow once the blow-up structure is established.

sourceIssues.reason: With (e_{−i}, e_j) = δ_{ij} and the displayed ordering, f_j = e_j + Σ_k A_{kj} e_{−(s+1−k)} + v_j e_0, so (f_i, f_j) = A_{s+1−i,j} + (A_{s+1−j,i})^c + v_i^c v_j (form conjugate-linear in the first variable; the other convention gives the same index reversal), i.e. J_sA + ᵗ(J_sA)^c + ᵗv^c v = 0. sourceIssues.locator: Lemma C.2.2(2) (published p. 355), Lemma C.2.4 (p. 360), and proofs of Lemma C.2.2(1) (p. 357), C.2.2(2) (p. 358), C.2.4 (p. 361); arXiv v3 p. 165–169
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts existence of (α_2, …, α_r) ∈ (ℂ^×)^{r−1}, determined up to permutation, with 1 ⩽ |α_2| ⩽ ⋯ ⩽ |α_r|. It asserts that I^{GL_{2r}}(α̲_r^{−1} ⊠ ⋯ ⊠ α̲_2^{−1} ⊠ St_2 ⊠ α̲_2 ⊠ ⋯ ⊠ α̲_r) has a unique irreducible quotient isomorphic to BC(π).
sourceIssues.correction: 'unique up to permutation and up to replacing α_i by α_i^{−1} when |α_i| = 1', i.e. unique up to the Weyl group of type BC_{r−1} (resp. BC_r in the proof of Lemma C.2.2(1)).
sourceIssues.reason: For r = 2 and α_2 = i, the choices α_2 = i and α_2 = −i = i^{−1} both satisfy 1 ⩽ |α_2| and give I^{GL_4}(−i̲ ⊠ St_2 ⊠ i̲) ≅ I^{GL_4}(i̲ ⊠ St_2 ⊠ −i̲) (irreducible tempered induction, invariant under permuting the inducing data), but (i) and (−i) are not permutations of each other. So uniqueness 'up to permutation' is false whenever some α_i is unimodular and ≠ ±1. Defence: the intended uniqueness (up to the obvious symmetry) is clear, and the uniqueness clause is never used (Proposition C.2.5 compares Satake parameters). Independent check: Quote checked on p. 355 (Lemma C.2.2(2)), p. 360 (Lemma C.2.4), p. 357 (proof of C.2.2(1): 'α_i ∉ {−1, q}, unique up to permutation'), p. 358 and p. 361. The first reading's counterexample holds. For r = 2 and |α_2| = 1 with α_2 ≠ ±1, both α_2 and α_2^{−1} satisfy 1 ⩽ |α_2|. The unitarily induced I^{GL_4}(α_2^{−1} ⊠ St_2 ⊠ α_2) is irreducible and invariant under permuting the inducing data, so both choices work, and they are not permutations of each other. The true uniqueness is up to the Weyl group {±1}^{r−1} ⋊ 𝔖_{r−1}, with the normalisation |α_i| ⩾ 1 removing the sign only when |α_i| > 1. The clause is never used: Proposition C.2.5 compares BC(π) with BC(π′) directly, and the intended statement is clear and true. So this is a misprint with no consequences. Versions: v2/v3 identical; v1 has the same ambiguity for multi-subsets {s_i} with Re s_i ⩾ 0.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Lemma C.2.4, displayed formula for C(α), published p. 362; arXiv v3 p. 169
sourceIssues.printed: The source uses continuity and [15, Theorem 3.1] to assert T_wφ′_α = C(α)φ′_{wα}, with nonzero C(α) = ∏_{i=r_0+1}^{r} ( (α_i − q^{−1})/(α_i − 1) ∏_{|α_j|<|α_i|} (α_i − q^{−2}α_j)/(α_i − α_j) ∏_{j=1}^{i−1} (α_iα_j − q^{−2})/(α_iα_j − 1) ).
sourceIssues.correction: Add 'where α_1 := q' (as in the proof of Lemma C.2.2(2)) and restrict the middle product to j ⩾ 2. Equivalently, C(α) = ∏_{i=r_0+1}^{r} ( (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − 1) · ∏_{j⩾2, |α_j|<|α_i|} (α_i − q^{−2}α_j)/(α_i − α_j) · ∏_{j=2}^{i−1} (α_iα_j − q^{−2})/(α_iα_j − 1) ).
sourceIssues.reason: Rank-one check r = 2, r_0 = 1: G = U(V′_4), V′_4 = H ⊕ V′_2 with V′_2 anisotropic. For the torus t_a (a on e_2, ā^{−1} on e_{−2}) the unipotent radical of P_min has F⁺-dimension 4 + 1 with weights ā^{−1} and N(a)^{−1}, so δ_{P_min}(t_ϖ) = |ϖ|_F^{−3} = q^6 and the trivial representation is a subrepresentation of I(𝟏′_2 ⊠ α̲_2) at α_2 = q^{−3}. The long intertwining operator must kill the spherical vector there (otherwise T_w would be an isomorphism I(q^{−3}) ≅ I(q^3), impossible since 𝟏 is a sub of the first and not of the second), so C must vanish at α_2 = q^{−3}; the printed C = (α_2 − q^{−1})/(α_2 − 1)·[undefined j = 1 term] does not (without the j = 1 term it is finite and nonzero at q^{−3}). Macdonald's formula confirms: both maximal parahorics of U(V′_4) (stabilizers of vertex lattices of type 1 and 3) have reductive quotient U_1 × U_3 over 𝔽_q, so the Iwahori–Hecke algebra has both parameters q^3 (|U_3(𝔽_q)/B| = q^3 + 1) and c(α) = (α − q^{−3})/(α − 1), the analogue of (α − q^{−1})/(α − 1) for U(1,1) whose vertices have parameter q. With α_1 := q the printed j = 1 factor is (qα_i − q^{−2})/(qα_i − 1) = (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − q^{−1}), and (α_i − q^{−1})/(α_i − 1) times it gives (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − 1). Defence: only C(α) ≠ 0 is used, and every factor of the correct formula is finite and nonzero for |α_i| > 1, so Lemma C.2.4 is unaffected. Independent check: Quote checked on p. 362. α = (α_2,…,α_r), so α_1 in ∏_{j=1}^{i−1} is undefined. The first reading's computation of the correct long-root factor is right. U(V′_4) has relative root system BC_1 with root spaces of F⁺-dimension 4 and 1, so δ^{1/2}(t_ϖ) = q^{±3}. Its two maximal parahorics (vertex lattices of types 1 and 3) both have reductive quotient U_1 × U_3 over 𝔽_q, and [K:I] = q³+1. So c = (α − q^{−3})/(α − 1), which vanishes where the trivial representation embeds. The first reading also shows that the printed formula is exactly correct if α_1 := q, as in Lemma C.2.2(2), where α = (q, α_2, …, α_r) on p. 358: (α_i − q^{−1})/(α_i − 1) · (qα_i − q^{−2})/(qα_i − 1) = (α_i − q^{−3})/(α_i − 1). That reading is the natural one: BC(𝟏′_2) = St_2 has parameters {q, q^{−1}}, and the formula copies the C.2.2(2) formula, where the middle product is written over j > 1. The version history supports this. v1 p. 169 printed the U(1,1) factor (1 − q^{−1−2s_i})/(1 − q^{−2s_i}) with no j = 1 term, which really was wrong. v2 p. 170 added ∏_{j=1}^{i−1}, which with s_1 = 1/2 (α_1 = q) turns (1 − q^{−1−2s_i}) into (1 − q^{−3−2s_i}): a repair whose α_1 was never written down. So the published formula is correct up to an undefined symbol (α_1 = q) and an implicit j ⩾ 2 in the middle product. That makes it a misprint, not an error. The alternative reading, which drops j = 1, is the v1 error. Only C(α) ≠ 0 is used, and it holds under every reading, so 'nothing' is right.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Proposition D.1.3, published p. 366 (definition of K_{w_0,0}); arXiv v3 p. 172
sourceIssues.printed: The source takes w_0 to be the rational prime below w and defines K_{w_0,0} := ∏_{v|w_0} U(Λ)(O_{F⁺_v}), describing it as hyperspecial maximal in G(ℚ_{w_0}).
sourceIssues.correction: Either add to Proposition D.1.3 the hypothesis that no place of F⁺ above the rational prime w_0 below w lies in Σ⁺ (i.e. w_0 ∉ Σ := {p | Σ⁺_p ∩ Σ⁺ ≠ ∅}), or explain how to treat places v | w_0, v ≠ w, lying in Σ⁺ (where V_v may be non-split and K_v arbitrary). For Corollary D.1.4 the extra hypothesis is harmless: Chebotarev supplies infinitely many admissible w, hence w with w_0 not below any given finite Σ⁺′.
sourceIssues.reason: The statement only requires w ∉ Σ⁺ ∪ Σ⁺_ℓ with w split in F; other places v of F⁺ above w_0 may belong to Σ⁺ (Σ⁺ is an arbitrary finite set containing Σ⁺_bad). For such v, Λ is only given away from Σ⁺ (U(Λ)(O_{F⁺_v}) is undefined), V_v need not be split, and K_v is an arbitrary factor of K_{Σ⁺}; then K_{w_0,0} is not defined/hyperspecial, G_{ℚ_{w_0}} may be non-quasi-split, and the smooth integral model 𝒮(G̃, h̃)_{K^{w_0}} over W(F̄_{w_0}), the Igusa varieties and the Mantovan formula used afterwards are not available as described. The subsequent definitions (Σ := {p | Σ⁺_p ∩ Σ⁺ ≠ ∅}, (K_T)_p maximal for p ∉ Σ, test functions φ_Σ ⊗ φ^Σ on G(𝔸^{∞,w_0}) × J_b(ℚ_{w_0})) are consistent only with w_0 ∉ Σ. Note w_0 is automatically unramified in F (else Σ⁺_{w_0} ⊆ Σ⁺_bad ⊆ Σ⁺, contradicting w ∉ Σ⁺). Defence: Hodge cocharacter μ is trivial at the places v | w_0 other than w, so a variant with non-hyperspecial level at those places might be made to work, and the only application (Corollary D.1.4) can choose w with w_0 ∉ Σ; but as written the proposition is proved only under the extra hypothesis. Independent check: Quote checked on p. 366. Proposition D.1.3 (p. 365) allows any finite Σ⁺ ⊇ Σ⁺_bad, requires V_v split only for v ∉ Σ⁺_∞ ∪ Σ⁺, and only asks that w ∉ Σ⁺ ∪ Σ⁺_ℓ with w split in F. Nothing prevents another place v | w_0 from lying in Σ⁺. For such v, Λ (given only away from Σ⁺) is undefined, U(V_v) need not be quasi-split, and K_v is an arbitrary factor of K_{Σ⁺}. So K_{w_0,0} := ∏_{v|w_0} U(Λ)(O_{F⁺_v}) is neither defined nor hyperspecial, and the smooth projective model 𝒮(G̃, h̃)_{K^{w_0}} over W(F̄_{w_0}) and the Mantovan/Igusa argument are unavailable as written. Shrinking K_v does not help with F̄_ℓ coefficients and non-hyperspecial targets. The rest of the proof (Σ := {p | Σ⁺_p ∩ Σ⁺ ≠ ∅}, (K_T)_p maximal for p ∉ Σ, test functions φ_Σ ⊗ φ^Σ on G(𝔸^{∞,w_0}) × J_b(ℚ_{w_0}), p. 367) is consistent only with w_0 ∉ Σ. Σ⁺_bad is the union of the Σ⁺_p for p ramified in F (p. 120), so w_0 is unramified in F, as the first reading says. Reach: D.1.3 is used only in Corollary D.1.4 (p. 368), whose proof produces infinitely many admissible w, so one can take w_0 ∉ Σ for any given Σ⁺′ (as Definition D.1.1 requires). Footnote 9 (p. 146) and the introduction's remark on p. 110 refer only to the method. The statement is probably true by a variant with non-hyperspecial level at the definite places above w_0, but it is proved only under the extra hypothesis. Versions: same sentence in v1 (Theorem D.1.3) p. 171, v2 p. 172, v3 p. 172.

sourceIssues.locator: Proof of Corollary D.1.4, published p. 368; arXiv v3 p. 173
sourceIssues.printed: The source asserts α_i/α_j ∉ {1, ‖w‖} for i ≠ j in F̄_ℓ whenever the rational prime ℓ is sufficiently large. Choosing a prime λ of E over ℓ, it applies Chebotarev to any residual ρ̄_{Π,λ} of ρ_{Π,λ} to obtain infinitely many nonarchimedean w of F⁺ outside Σ⁺ ∪ Σ⁺_ℓ, split in F, for which (D.1) is decomposed generic at w.
sourceIssues.correction: Apply Chebotarev to ρ̄_{Π,λ} × ε̄_ℓ (i.e. in the compositum of the field cut out by ρ̄_{Π,λ} with F(ζ_ℓ)), producing places u of F of degree one over ℚ with ρ̄_{Π,λ}(Frob_u) conjugate to ρ̄_{Π,λ}(Frob_w) and ‖u‖ ≡ ‖w‖ (mod ℓ); then the ratios of the roots of φ(H_{u|_{F⁺}}) are the α_i/α_j mod λ, which avoid 1 and ‖u‖.
sourceIssues.reason: Decomposed genericity at the new place w′ = u|_{F⁺} requires that no ratio of roots equals ‖w′‖ in F̄_ℓ. Conjugacy of ρ̄(Frob_u) with ρ̄(Frob_w) controls the ratios (they equal α_i/α_j mod λ) but not ‖u‖ mod ℓ; ε̄_ℓ(Frob_u) is not determined by ρ̄_{Π,λ}(Frob_u) (conjugate self-duality relates Frob_u and Frob_{u^c}, not ε̄_ℓ(Frob_u) alone). So ratio ≠ ‖w‖ does not give ratio ≠ ‖w′‖ unless ‖w′‖ ≡ ‖w‖ mod ℓ is also imposed. Defence: the fix is routine and standard; the conclusion is correct.
